atilogwu.name: Atilogwu
atilogwu.tagline: Nigeria — spirited youth dance from the Igbo ethnic group of Nigeria that focuses on vigorous body movement and often in
atilogwu.profile: Atilogwu is a spirited youth dance from the Igbo ethnic group of Nigeria that focuses on vigorous body movement and often includes acrobatics. In the Igbo language, the word itself "Atilogwu" translates into "has magic, as in sorcery/witchcraft". The name stems from rumors that bewitchment or magic potions had to be involved if the children of the village could perform so exuberantly and energetically, while making it look so effortless. The tempo of the dance matches the tempo of the music, which is dependent on the beat of the drum and ogene, a metal gong instrument.
atilogwu.insight: Atilogwu is a spirited youth dance from the Igbo ethnic group of Nigeria that focuses on vigorous body movement and often includes acrobatics.

azonto.name: Azonto
azonto.tagline: Communicative Ghanaian street dance and music genre from Accra
azonto.profile: Azonto is a dance and music genre from Ghana connected to the traditional Ga dance Kpanlogo, associated with coastal Greater Accra towns such as Chorkor, James Town, Teshie, Nungua and Tema (Wikipedia). Several accounts say it was formerly known as 'Apaa' ('work'); its hand movements mimic everyday activities (washing, driving, ironing, praying). One foot is planted while the other pivots on the ball; the hands trace flowing circular motions (Wikipedia). Per Red Bull, following Sarkodie and E.L.'s 2011 'U Go Kill Me', the Azonto craze rapidly took over Ghana and African diaspora communities in the UK and US.
azonto.insight: Popular-music researcher Jesse Weaver Shipley argues that, like hiplife, Azonto's popularity stems from diaspora interactions - identified with Ghanaian indigeneity by those abroad and with cosmopolitanism by those at home (Wikipedia).

atsiapat.tagline: Greece — Atsiapat (Pontic: Άτσιαπατ), also spelt atsapat (Άτσαπατ), is the first in a sequence of three Pontic Greek ma
atsiapat.profile: Atsiapat (Pontic: Άτσιαπατ), also spelt atsapat (Άτσαπατ), is the first in a sequence of three Pontic Greek male dances performed in the region of Pontus, as well as by refugees of Pontos. Atsapat is characterized by short steps and exaggerated movements that resemble stretching. This dance is followed directly by Serra. The final dance in the sequence is the Pyrrhichios. Atsapat is the Greek pronunciation of the Pontic Turkish city of Akçaabat. The region is famous for the virtuosity of its Pyrrhichios dancers.

attan.name: Attan
attan.era: Ancient; possible Zoroastrian/pre-Islamic roots, codified over centuries
attan.tagline: Afghanistan's whirling circle dance, drum-driven and proudly national
attan.profile: Attan is the national dance of Afghanistan, originating among Pashtun tribes of southern and eastern Afghanistan and northwestern Pakistan. Dancers form a circle around a dohol (double-headed barrel drum) player, beginning with slow steps that accelerate, with spins, hand-claps, head and hair flicks, and handkerchiefs; a performance can last 5 to 30 minutes (Wikipedia; Britannica). Once danced by warriors before battle, it now features at weddings, engagements and Nowruz; regional styles include Kabuli, Logari, Paktia/Khosti, Wardaki, Kandahari and Herati.
attan.insight: Britannica notes the open-air Attan "became the national dance of the Pashtun and then of the entire country," and it was banned under the Taliban; Afghanistan has applied to UNESCO to register it (Arab News), making it a potent emblem of Afghan identity, though it has not yet been inscribed.

bagurumba.name: Bagurumba
bagurumba.tagline: The Bodo 'butterfly dance' mirroring nature's grace
bagurumba.profile: Bagurumba is a traditional dance of the indigenous Bodo (Boro) people of Assam, nicknamed the 'butterfly dance' because its slow, poised movements imitate butterflies, birds and swaying flowers (Wikipedia). Performed mainly by women during the spring festival Bwishagu (mid-April), dancers wear the colourful handwoven dokhona, jwmgra (fasra) and aronai, using the jwmgra cloth like butterfly wings. It is accompanied by instruments including the sifung (long bamboo flute), serja (bowed instrument), kham (drum), jota and gongwna (Wikipedia; The Better India).
bagurumba.insight: At 'Bagurumba Dwhou 2026', held 17 January 2026 in Guwahati, over 10,000 artistes - including roughly 8,000 dancers drawn from 81 assembly constituencies across 23 districts - performed together (The Meghalayan Express; narendramodi.in).

asyik.name: Asyik
asyik.tagline: classical royal court dance popular in Patani and Kelantan
asyik.profile: Asyik (literally "beloved"/"besotted") is a classical royal court dance popular in Patani and Kelantan. According to Hikayat Patani, the dance was created in 1644 to entertain the grieving Ratu Kuning over the loss of her favorite bird. The dance's name "the beloved" could have been referring to the lost bird. The performance begins with ten beautifully costumed dancers entering the dancing hall and sitting gracefully. The prima donna, also known as Puteri Asyik ("the princess of love") will then appear and the dance begins with gracious and delicate body movements and gestures.
asyik.insight: Asyik (literally "beloved"/"besotted") is a classical royal court dance popular in Patani and Kelantan.

balboa.profile: The Balboa, also known as "Bal", is a swing dance that emerged in Southern California during the early 1930s as a response to swing music. The earliest recorded reference to Balboa is 1932. This date coincides with what is generally accepted to be the beginning of swing. The dance enjoyed huge popularity in California during the 1930s and 1940s, and was still being danced by original dancers into the 21st century. Balboa is a social partner dance that distinctively relies on closed position. The earliest form of the dance emerged in the high schools and dance venues of southern California.
balboa.insight: It was created for the Panama Californian Exhibition, Balboa Park, 1915-17, with illustrated instructions published in newspapers.

baile-de-la-conquista.profile: The Baile de la Conquista or Dance of the Conquest is a traditional folkloric dance from Guatemala. The dance reenacts the invasion led by Spanish conquistador Pedro de Alvarado and his confrontation with Tecun Uman, ruler of K'iche' kingdom of Q'umarkaj. Although the dance is more closely associated with Guatemalan traditions, it has been performed in early colonial regions of Latin America at the urging of Catholic friars and priests, as a method of converting various native populations and African slaves to the Catholic Church.

bajidor-kahot.name: Bajidor Kahot
bajidor-kahot.tagline: Modern Sundanese dance fusing Ketuk Tilu and Jaipongan
bajidor-kahot.profile: Bajidor Kahot is a modern Sundanese created group dance from West Java which combines the dance movements of Ketuk Tilu and Jaipongan as the basis of its motions (Wikipedia). It was created around the year 2000 and is typically performed by young women in brightly colored Sundanese kebaya using fans (kipas) and scarves (selendang), shifting through dynamic formations. The dance is accompanied by Sundanese kendang drumming and gamelan, and its roots trace to the older Kliningan-Bajidoran folk performance of the Karawang and Subang regions.
bajidor-kahot.insight: As an 'invented tradition,' Bajidor Kahot exemplifies how late-20th-century choreographers repackaged Sundanese folk vocabulary into accessible stage repertoire (Budaya-Indonesia).

It is also sometimes spelled in English as 'beledi' or 'baladee'. In Egypt, the term baladi does not only apply to local music and dance, and can also apply to many other things that are considered native, rustic or traditional, for example 'baladi bread' or 'Aish Baladi".

baishou-dance.name: Baishou Dance
baishou-dance.profile: The Baishou Dance (摆手舞, baishouwu, 'hand-waving dance') is a group ritual dance of the Tujia people of Xiangxi, Hunan. Per English Wikipedia, 'It originates from an ancestor worship ceremony and dates back nearly 1,000 years ago, according to the broken stele in the Temple of Eight Clan Leaders (Qing Dynasty) and the county annals.' It uses 70 ritual gestures to represent war, farming, hunting, courtship and other aspects of traditional life, accompanied by gongs and drums. Per the Department of Culture and Tourism of Hunan Province, 'Grand Baishou is performed by over 1,000 dancers when offering sacrifices to the ancestors of the whole group.'
baishou-dance.insight: It is one of China's oldest continuous folk dances and a key carrier of Tujia history, recognized as national intangible cultural heritage (Hunan provincial government).

ball-dels-cossiers.name: Ball dels Cossiers
ball-dels-cossiers.tagline: Spain — most popular traditional dance on the island of Majorca, in the Spanish Balearic Islands
ball-dels-cossiers.profile: The Ball dels Cossiers (Catalan for "Dance of the Cossiers") is the most popular traditional dance on the island of Majorca, in the Spanish Balearic Islands. In the dance, three pairs of dancers, who are typically male, defend a representation of good, the "Lady," who is played by a man or a woman, from a demon. Normally the dance is done in a circle, with the Lady in the center, although some more solemn dance troupes (such as La Oferta, the Mocadors, the Bandanas, or the Mercançó) deviate from this tradition.

baris.profile: Baris is a family of traditional Balinese war dances accompanied by gamelan, in which dancers depict the feelings of a young warrior prior to battle and glorify the warrior's commanding presence (Wikipedia). The name derives from 'bebarisan,' meaning line or file formation, referring to soldiers who served the ancient rajas of Bali. There is a non-ritual solo form (baris tunggal), often the first dance a budding dancer learns, and over thirty ritual group types named for the weapons carried (spear, shield, arrow, kris). The ritual Baris Upacara is a sacred wali dance used in temple ceremonies.
baris.insight: Baris Upacara is one of the nine dances within the three Balinese genres inscribed by UNESCO in 2015, performed as an offering to welcome gods and ancestors (Jakarta Post).

ballu-tundu.profile: Ballu tundu or ballu sardu is a traditional Sardinian folk dance which is typically danced in a closed or open circle. The dance was described as early as 1805 by Mameli and by La Marmora in 1825. In northern and central Sardinia, the dance is lively and animated with leaps and agile movements and usually accompanied by a choir of three or more singers in the center of the circle. In other areas, the dance is done to launeddas and the shepherd's sulittu, but the accordion had also made its appearance by the 19th century. The introduction is in 24 time but the dance itself is done in 68.

bardo-chham.name: Bardo Chham
bardo-chham.tagline: Masked dance of good versus evil zodiac animals
bardo-chham.profile: Bardo Chham is a folk dance of the Sherdukpen (and Monpa) Buddhist communities of West Kameng, Arunachal Pradesh, rooted in Tibetan Buddhism - 'Bardo' is the intermediate state between death and rebirth and 'Chham' means dance (Wikipedia). Based on the triumph of good over evil, the dance holds that twelve evil forces appear as animals through the year; performers don colourful wooden animal masks representing the zodiac and dance to a large frame drum and cymbals to fight these forces. It is interpreted locally as 'dance of the zodiac' and performed by both men and women on festive occasions (History of Monyul; Gosahin).
bardo-chham.insight: The dance survives through oral transmission within the small Sherdukpen tribe, with no formal training schools, making it a fragile vehicle of the community's cosmology and Buddhist moral teaching (DanceAsk; Saralstudy).

basse-danse.profile: The basse danse, or "low dance", was a popular court dance in the 15th and early 16th centuries, especially at the Burgundian court. The word basse describes the nature of the dance, in which partners move quietly and gracefully in a slow gliding or walking motion without leaving the floor, while in livelier dances both feet left the floor in jumps or leaps. The basse danse was a precursor of the pavane as a dignified processional dance. The term may apply to the dance or the music alone.

bedara-vesha.profile: Bedara Vesha ('Hunter Dance') is a folk dance performed on the nights before Holi in Sirsi town, Uttara Kannada, Karnataka, staged every alternate year and drawing large crowds across five days (Wikipedia). It is tied to a roughly 300-year-old legend from the Sonda dynasty era about the warrior Malleshi of the Beda community. Around 50 solo artists perform in elaborate costume - including a giant bundle of peacock feathers restrained by ropes - accompanied by whistle-blowers and tamate (hand-drum) beaters, performing through the night and culminating at the Shri Marikamba Temple (Satyaagrah; MetroSaga).
bedara-vesha.insight: Dollu Kunitha is also performed during the Bedara Vesha festivities, and one performer is traditionally barred from looking another in the face, underscoring the ritual discipline behind the spectacle (Satyaagrah).

bear-dance.tagline: Spain, 15th century — Ute ceremonial dance that occurs in the spring
bear-dance.profile: Bear Dance is a Ute ceremonial dance that occurs in the spring. It is a ten-day event to strengthen social ties within the community, encourage courtship, and mark the end of puberty for girls. The event includes dancing, feasting, games, horse racing, and gambling. It is one of the oldest Ute ceremonies. The Bear Dance was first recorded by Spanish conquistadors in the 15th century, but oral tradition dates it to be a thousand years old or older. and continues to be performed by modern Ute. The bear symbolizes leadership, strength, and wisdom.
bear-dance.insight: Bear Dance is a Ute ceremonial dance that occurs in the spring.

bedhaya.tagline: Sacred Javanese court dance of refined alus character
bedhaya.profile: The bedhaya is a sacred, ritualized Javanese court dance associated with the royal palaces of Yogyakarta and Surakarta (Wikipedia). Along with the srimpi, it epitomized the elegant (alus) character of the royal court and became an important symbol of the ruler's power. It is performed by nine female dancers, relatives or wives of the Susuhunan, before a private audience. The modern form is traditionally dated to the court of Sultan Agung of Mataram, though it was not clearly documented until the late 18th century. Origin myths involve either a Hindu deity creating the nine dancers or Kanjeng Ratu Kidul, Goddess of the Southern Sea.
bedhaya.insight: The bedhaya takes distinct forms in each court city - the Bedhaya Ketawang of Surakarta and the Bedhaya Semang of Yogyakarta, the latter unperformed for over two decades (Wikipedia).

bihu-dance.profile: The Bihu dance is an indigenous folk dance of Assam tied to the Bihu festival, especially the spring Rongali/Bohag Bihu in mid-April (Wikipedia). Performed by groups of young men and women, it is characterized by brisk steps, rapid hand movements and rhythmic hip-swaying, traditionally serving as a courtship dance and celebrating fertility and the new agricultural season (Wikipedia). Dancers wear red-themed traditional Assamese attire (mekhela sador for women) and perform to instruments such as the dhol and pepa (hornpipe) (Britannica).
bihu-dance.insight: The first official record of Bihu dance is said to be Ahom king Rudra Singha inviting dancers to the Rang Ghar fields around 1694; it was first brought to the urban stage in Guwahati in 1962 (Wikipedia).

berd.profile: Berd (Բերդ, also Berdapar), meaning "fortress," is an Armenian military folk dance famous for a circle of men standing on the shoulders of another circle to create a rotating human tower (Armenian dance, Wikipedia; NaTakallam). It originates from the old Armenian region of Vaspurakan near Lake Van in Western Armenia, and is said to derive from a game called gmbetakhagh ("dome game"). Performed by men to drum and zurna, it dramatizes the storming and defense of a fortress.
berd.insight: Berd vividly literalizes the idea of collective strength: by physically constructing a "fortress" from interlocked bodies, the dance enacts community defense and unity, themes deeply tied to Armenian highland history (NaTakallam).

bizhu-dance.profile: Bizhu (also Bizu/Bijhu) is the most popular dance of the Chakma people, performed during their three-day Bizu New Year festival around 12-14 April, marking Chaitra-Sankranti, the last day of the Bengali calendar (Wikipedia; Tripura State Portal). The dance climaxes the second day, Mul Bizhu, and is thought to have originated as a devotional offering performed within Chakma temple precincts; it is a group dance with participants aligned in square or circular patterns and is marked by abrupt pauses (Wikipedia). It is accompanied by flutes and drums including the dhol, baajhi, kheng-garang and dhuduk; women wear flowers and silver ornaments (Wikipedia; Tripura State Portal).
bizhu-dance.insight: Originally rooted in jhum (shifting) cultivation as a propitiation of the earth for a good harvest, Bizhu has in recent decades lost some agrarian linkages and become primarily a social celebration of Chakma identity (Wikipedia).

bhagavata-mela.tagline: Tamil Nadu's Vaishnava temple dance-drama of Melattur
bhagavata-mela.profile: Bhagavata Mela is a classical dance-drama tradition of Tamil Nadu, especially Melattur near Thanjavur, performed as an annual Vaishnavite temple offering, primarily to Lord Lakshmi Narasimha (Wikipedia). It descends from Kuchipudi: after the fall of the Vijayanagara Empire (~1565), some Telugu Brahmin dance-drama families migrated south and were granted land by king Achuthappa Nayak, evolving the Kuchipudi-inspired form into Bhagavata Mela. Traditionally enacted entirely by male Brahmins (including female roles), beginning after dusk by oil lamps, it combines Nritta, Nritya and Natya set to Carnatic music, drawing on the Natya Shastra (Wikipedia; Melattur Bhagavata Mela).
bhagavata-mela.insight: Its core repertoire is the ten Telugu dance-dramas of Melattur Venkatarama Sastri (1743-1809), of which 'Prahlada Charitram', performed on Narasimha Jayanti, is the most enduring (DT Next; The Verandah Club).

It has its roots in African-American dance, which itself is rooted in sub-Saharan African music traditions and the historical dances brought to the United States by European immigrants. Boogaloo originated in New York City mainly by stateside Cubans and Puerto Ricans with African American music influences. The style was a fusion of popular African American jazz, rhythm and blues (R&B) and soul music with mambo and son montuno, with songs in both English and Spanish. bollywood.profile: Bollywood dance is the popular film-derived dance style of Hindi cinema, a synthesis of Indian classical (Kathak, Bharatanatyam) and folk traditions (bhangra, garba) fused with Western forms such as jazz, disco and hip-hop (Wikipedia). It evolved with the rise of Indian cinema in the early 20th century; the term 'Bollywood' (Bombay + Hollywood) was coined in the 1970s when the conventions of commercial masala Hindi films were established, with Yaadon Ki Baarat (1973) cited as the first quintessentially Bollywood film (Wikipedia). Group choreography, expressive facial gestures and synchronization to playback songs make it a global cultural phenomenon.
bollywood.insight: Performers such as Helen, often called Bollywood's first 'item girl', helped blend Western cabaret and disco with Indian elements, and Hindi dance music reached global audiences through tracks such as 'Jai Ho', which won the Academy Award for Best Original Song on 22 February 2009 (Wikipedia).

borborbor.profile: Borborbor (also Akpese) is a Ghanaian and Togolese recreational dance performed by the Ewe of the mid-Volta Region of Ghana and southern Togo, including Kpalime and Lome (Wikipedia). Per Wikipedia, it is believed to have been originated by Mr. Francis Kudzo Nuatro in the 1950s, and is associated with Kpando, Ho, Hohoe and Peki. Mainly performed by women in colorful long garments twirling two white handkerchiefs, it features circular formations, waist turns and uplifting drum rhythms using vuga (master drum), asivu (support), vuvi, castanets and rattles (Wikipedia; Graphic Online).
borborbor.insight: Cultural authorities describe Borborbor as a unifying, non-discriminatory dance now performed in churches and at state events - including as a curtain-raiser at Independence Day at Ho's Jubilee Park (Graphic Online).

walking-boston.name: Walking Boston
walking-boston.tagline: The Walking Boston, sometimes designated the One Step Waltz, is a very simple dance in which many graceful fig
walking-boston.profile: The Walking Boston, sometimes designated the One Step Waltz, is a very simple dance in which many graceful figures may be introduced. It is done to the same music as the Hesitation Waltz and Dream Waltz. The man starts forward with his left foot and the lady backward with her right, simply walking to waltz time, counting one, two, three to each step. At each step the dancers rise on their toes. Four of these steps are taken forward (backward by the lady), then they balance backward and forward.
walking-boston.insight: The Walking Boston, sometimes designated the One Step Waltz, is a very simple dance in which many graceful figures may be introduced.

branle.profile: A branle ( BRAN-əl, BRAHL, French: [bʁɑ̃l] ), also bransle, brangle, brawl(e), brall(e), braul(e), brando (in Italy), bran (in Spain), or brantle (in Scotland), is a type of French dance popular from the early 16th century to the present, danced by couples in either a line or a circle. bugaku.name: Bugaku
bugaku.tagline: Stately masked court dance performed to gagaku music
bugaku.profile: Bugaku is the ceremonial court dance of Japan, performed to gagaku music for over twelve hundred years, marked by slow, precise and regal movements, elaborate embroidered costumes and masks, on a roughly 6-by-6-yard platform (Wikipedia, Bugaku). Britannica describes its two basic forms: 'dances of the left' (saho no mai), accompanied by togaku derived from Chinese music and danced in red costumes, and 'dances of the right' (uho no mai), accompanied by komagaku from Korea in blue/green costumes, often performed alternately as paired dances (tsugaimai) (Britannica).
bugaku.insight: Britannica notes Bugaku's repertoire derives from dance forms imported from China, Korea, India and Southeast Asia - making it, with its allied music gagaku, among the oldest surviving court dance-and-music traditions in the world.

breakaway.name: Breakaway
breakaway.tagline: Turkey, 1927 — Breakaway (Break-A-Way) was a swing dance, originally a syncopated Two-step
breakaway.profile: Breakaway (Break-A-Way) was a swing dance, originally a syncopated Two-step. In the Polka, a step called the Coquette (Love Chase) is defined as "The lady escapes from her partner and polkas solo while the gent pursues her, arms akimbo." The Break-Away was the name of swing before being named the Lindy Hop by Shorty George in 1927. The Breakaway was a cross between the "Texas Tommy, Two-step, Apache Dance, Turkey Trot, Cakewalk and Grizzly Bear.
breakaway.insight: Breakaway (Break-A-Way) was a swing dance, originally a syncopated Two-step.

bump.name: Bump
bump.tagline: United States — form of popular dance introduced in the 1970s in the United States
bump.profile: The Bump is a form of popular dance introduced in the 1970s in the United States. Two partners, generally one male and one female, bump their hips against each other to the beat of the song. Sometimes the dance can be more suggestive, with the female dancer bumping her hip against the male dancer's crotch. For this reason, the Bump is often believed to be the precursor to the erotic and controversial dance grinding. It is also known as the disco couple dance.
bump.insight: The Bump is a form of popular dance introduced in the 1970s in the United States.

bugg.name: Bugg
bugg.tagline: Sweden — common dance style in Sweden and is very popular on the dance floors when dansbands play
bugg.profile: Bugg is a common dance style in Sweden and is very popular on the dance floors when dansbands play. Bugg is a dance in 44 time and performed at different paces (120–180 beats per minute). Bugg is a partner dance and follows certain basic rules, but is essentially improvised, with one partner following the other's lead. Acrobatic moves are not allowed on national or international dance competitions. Swedish bugg belongs to the swing dance family and closely resembles modern jive. Bugg is both a very popular social dance as well as a competitive dance in Sweden.
bugg.insight: Bugg is a common dance style in Sweden and is very popular on the dance floors when dansbands play.

breton-dance.name: Breton dance
breton-dance.era: Traditional (some forms medieval); revived from the late 1950s
breton-dance.tagline: Umbrella of traditional Breton folk dances of the fest-noz.
breton-dance.profile: Breton dance is the umbrella of traditional dance forms from Brittany, the Celtic region of France, mostly social group dances in chains and circles (Wikipedia). Jean-Michel Guilcher identified five 'mother-forms' of Lower Brittany - the gavotte (dans tro), the en dro/an dro, the dans Treger, the dans Leon and the dans plinn - from which hundreds of terroir variants developed. Dances are performed at fest-noz (night festival) and fest-deiz (day festival), accompanied by kan-ha-diskan call-and-response singing or by sonneur duos and instruments such as the biniou (bagpipe), bombarde, accordion, clarinet (treujenn-gaol) and, via bagadou, the Scottish bagpipe. Revival came with the Celtic Circles and the modern fest-noz, credited especially to Loeiz Ropars from the 1950s.
breton-dance.insight: The fest-noz - 'festive gathering based on the collective practice of traditional dances of Brittany' - was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in 2012 (decision 7.COM 11.13; file 00707). UNESCO notes about a thousand fest-noz take place every year (UNESCO).

butoh.name: Butoh
butoh.tagline: Avant-garde 'dance of darkness' born in post-war Japan
butoh.profile: Butoh is a form of Japanese dance theatre that arose in 1959 through the collaboration of its two founders, Tatsumi Hijikata and Kazuo Ohno (Wikipedia, Butoh). Originally called Ankoku Butoh ('dance of utter darkness'), it features playful and grotesque imagery, taboo subjects, extreme or absurd environments, and is traditionally performed in white body makeup with slow, hyper-controlled motion. The first piece, Kinjiki (Forbidden Colors) by Hijikata - based on Yukio Mishima's novel - premiered at a 1959 dance festival and caused a scandal that established Hijikata as an iconoclast.
butoh.insight: In Jean Viala and Nourit Masson-Sekine's study, Ohno is regarded as 'the soul of butoh' and Hijikata as 'the architect of butoh'; the form emerged as a deliberate reaction against Japanese dance that Hijikata felt merely imitated the West or Noh (Wikipedia).

kompa.name: Compas
kompa.tagline: Haiti, 1955 — Nemours Jean-Baptiste's invention. The smoothest two-step in the Caribbean.
kompa.profile: Compas (French pronunciation: [kɔ̃pa]; Haitian Creole: konpa dirèk; French: compas direct), also known as konpa or kompa, is a modern méringue dance music genre of Haiti. The genre was created by Nemours Jean-Baptiste following the creation of Ensemble Aux Callebasses in 1955, which became Ensemble Nemours Jean-Baptiste in 1957. The frequent tours of the many Haitian bands have cemented the style in all the Caribbean. Therefore, compas is the main music of several countries such as Dominica and the French Antilles.

ndombolo.name: Ndombolo
ndombolo.tagline: Fast hip-swaying soukous offshoot that conquered Africa
ndombolo.profile: Ndombolo (or dombolo) is a Congolese (DR Congo) dance-music genre that emerged from soukous in the mid-1990s, defined by fast, hip-swaying movements over the high-energy sebene. Per Wikipedia, it features lead and backing vocals, electric guitars, drum kit and the atalaku's chants; it was pioneered by bands such as Wenge Musica and stars Koffi Olomide, JB Mpiana and Werrason. Its provocative moves drew bans in several countries even as it dominated dancefloors across central, eastern and western Africa.
ndombolo.insight: Ndombolo became continental Africa's defining dance craze of the late 1990s and 2000s and seeded styles from coupe-decale to Angolan kuduro (Wikipedia; African Music Library).

dancehall.name: Dancehall
dancehall.tagline: Kingston, Jamaica, 1980s — reggae sped up and toasted over. Street poetry danced at sound-system parties from Spanish Town to Tokyo.
dancehall.profile: Dancehall is a genre of Jamaican popular music that originated in the late 1970s. Initially, dancehall was a more sparse version of reggae than the roots style, which had dominated much of the 1970s. This music genre was not officially named until the 1980s, when the two words Dance and Hall (referring to the common venue) were joined to form Dancehall, which was then promoted internationally for the first time. At that time digital instrumentation became more prevalent, changing the sound considerably, with digital dancehall (or "ragga") becoming increasingly characterized by faster rhythms.
dancehall.insight: Shabba Ranks became the first dancehall artist to win at the Grammy Awards with his debut album As Raw as Ever in 1991. It broke a five-year hiatus being the only Dancehall album to top the reggae charts sins Shaggy's Summer in Kingston in 2011.

kagura.name: Kagura
kagura.era: Ancient mythological origin (Ame-no-Uzume myth); codified from the Heian period onward
kagura.tagline: Sacred Shinto ceremonial dance offered to the kami
kagura.profile: Kagura ('god-entertainment') is a type of Shinto ritual ceremonial dance and music; the term contracts kami no kura ('seat of god'), indicating the presence of deities in the practice (Wikipedia). A major function is chinkon, the purifying and pacifying of the spirit (Wikipedia). According to the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, its origin lies in the myth of Ame-no-Uzume, whose dance lured the sun goddess Amaterasu from her cave (Britannica). Two broad forms exist: mikagura, performed at the imperial court and major shrines such as Kamo and Iwashimizu Hachiman-gu, and satokagura, the folk variants including Iwami Kagura and Takachiho Kagura (Wikipedia).
kagura.insight: Kagura is treated as a sacred art dedicated to the kami; scholars hold it predates and influenced Noh theatre, especially in its storytelling and reenactment forms (Wikipedia).

noh.name: Noh
noh.era: Mid-14th century (developed by Kan'ami and Zeami)
noh.tagline: Oldest surviving Japanese masked dance-drama theatre
noh.profile: Noh is a major form of classical Japanese dance-drama performed since the 14th century, developed by Kan'ami and his son Zeami, and is the oldest major theatre art still regularly performed (Wikipedia). It integrates masks, costumes and props in a dance-based performance requiring highly trained actors and musicians; the dance element is the mai (Wikipedia). Often based on traditional literature, its hero is frequently a supernatural being in human form narrating a story (UNESCO). Together with the comic kyogen it forms nogaku, proclaimed a UNESCO Masterpiece in 2001 and inscribed on the Representative List in 2008 as 'Nogaku theatre' (UNESCO).
noh.insight: Per Wikipedia, Noh masks are carved from blocks of Japanese cypress and there are 'approximately 450 different masks mostly based on sixty types, all of which have distinctive names,' each conveying shifting emotion through the actor's movement (Wikipedia).

yosakoi.name: Yosakoi
yosakoi.tagline: Modern high-energy team dance with naruko clappers
yosakoi.profile: Yosakoi is a dynamic style of Japanese group dance that originated in Kochi Prefecture in 1954, when the city held the first Yosakoi Matsuri to revitalize the local economy after the war (Wikipedia). It combines traditional Japanese dance movement with modern music and is performed by large costumed teams (Wikipedia). Dancers must hold naruko - small wooden clappers historically used by farmers to scare birds - and must dance while moving forward, while the music must include part of Eisaku Takemasa's 'Yosakoi Naruko Odori' song (Wikipedia). Takemasa released the copyright to the public, encouraging adaptation (Grokipedia). The style spread nationwide, notably to Sapporo's Yosakoi Soran Festival (Wikipedia).
yosakoi.insight: Sapporo's Yosakoi Soran Festival, per Hokkaido's official Domingo tourism site, 'began with 10 teams and 1,000 participants in 1992' and today 'sees around 30,000 participants from Japan and overseas, and attracts around 2 million spectators' (Domingo, Hokkaido).

jaipongan.name: Jaipongan
jaipongan.era: Created by Gugum Gumbira; public debut 1974
jaipongan.tagline: Energetic Sundanese social dance born of cultural revival
jaipongan.profile: Jaipongan (Jaipong) is a popular Sundanese dance of West Java created by composer-choreographer Gugum Gumbira, drawing on the traditional ketuk tilu social-dance music, pencak silat martial-arts movements, and the masked Topeng Banjet theater (Wikipedia). After President Sukarno's 1961 ban on Western music and his call to revive indigenous arts, Gumbira studied rural dance and festival music for twelve years. Jaipongan made its public debut in 1974, its first known works being 'Daun Pulus Keser Bojong' and 'Rendeng Bojong.' The name imitates the sounds of the ensemble's drums. It features virtuosic kendang drumming, flirtatious singing by a sinden, and energetic hip and shoulder movements.
jaipongan.insight: Spread by the 1970s-80s cassette boom and Gumbira's Jugala orchestra - notably the 1987 album 'Tonggeret' with singer Idjah Hadidjah - Jaipongan became West Java's emblematic dance despite official concern over its sensuality (Wikipedia; Grokipedia).

soran-bushi.name: Soran Bushi
soran-bushi.era: Late 19th-early 20th century herring-fishing work song; modern Nanchu Soran dance from the early 1990s
soran-bushi.tagline: Hokkaido herring-fishermen's sea shanty danced as net-hauling mime
soran-bushi.profile: Soran Bushi is one of Japan's most famous min'yo (folk songs) and its associated dance, a sea shanty first sung by herring fishermen of Hokkaido to coordinate hauling nets (Wikipedia). The dance mimes pulling in fishing nets, the rolling waves and hauling the catch, punctuated by the call-and-response refrains 'Dokkoisho!' and 'Soran!', words used to encourage the fishermen's labor (Wikipedia). It emerged during the herring 'Golden Age' of the Meiji and Taisho eras (Reiroh). The widely known modern version, Nanchu Soran, was developed for Wakkanai Minami Junior High School and spread nationwide through schools (Wikipedia).
soran-bushi.insight: Per Wikipedia, the Nanchu Soran choreography was developed by Butoh dancer Jusho Kasuga - acting out ocean waves, fishermen dragging nets, pulling ropes and lifting luggage over their shoulders - and the school won the Folk Song and Dance Awards honorable mention in 1992 and the Grand Prix of the Prime Minister of Japan in 1993 (Wikipedia).

contemporary-dance.name: Contemporary dance
contemporary-dance.tagline: Genre-blending concert dance born from modern dance and ballet
contemporary-dance.profile: Contemporary dance is a genre of concert dance that developed during the mid-twentieth century and has grown into one of the dominant genres for formally trained dancers worldwide, especially in the U.S. and Europe (Wikipedia). It evolved out of and in reaction to modern dance and ballet, drawing on the legacies of Martha Graham, Merce Cunningham - who presented his first solo New York concert in April 1944 with composer John Cage, his life partner and frequent collaborator until Cage's death in 1992 - and German Tanztheater figures such as Pina Bausch (Wikipedia; Merce Cunningham Trust). It blends ballet legwork with modern dance's torso emphasis, plus contract-release, floorwork, improvisation and release technique, and freely absorbs non-Western forms such as African dance and Japanese Butoh (Wikipedia).
contemporary-dance.insight: Per the New Grove and the International Encyclopedia of Dance, contemporary dance is defined less by fixed steps than by innovation and the collapse of distinctions between composition and improvisation (Wikipedia).

jazz-dance.name: Jazz dance
jazz-dance.tagline: A dynamic American dance evolving from African American vernacular to theatrical jazz styles.
jazz-dance.profile: Jazz dance originated in early 20th-century African American communities in the United States, evolving from social dances like the Charleston and Lindy hop into theatrical forms. It features grounded movement, torso mobility, and parallel foot positions, blending vernacular styles with ballet and modern dance techniques. Theatrical jazz was shaped by choreographers such as Jack Cole and Bob Fosse, while contemporary and commercial jazz incorporate pop and hip hop influences.
jazz-dance.insight: In 1917, jazz pianist Spencer Williams inspired the shimmy, a dance with shoulders quickly alternating back and forth, marking early jazz dance’s social roots.
jazz-dance.profile_long:
Jazz dance began in the early 1900s within African American communities in the United States, emerging alongside jazz music as a social dance form. Early vernacular jazz dances included the shimmy, Charleston, and Lindy hop, characterized by rhythmic, grounded movements and improvisation. The shimmy, inspired by Spencer Williams's 1917 song “Shim-Me-Sha-Wabble,” involved rapid shoulder alternations while keeping the body still. The Charleston featured toes-in, heels-out twisting steps, performed solo or in groups, while the Lindy hop was a spontaneous, rhythmically complex partner dance. During the Great Depression, these dances flourished as popular social outlets.

From the 1940s onward, jazz dance transitioned into theatrical performance, with choreographers like Jack Cole, Bob Fosse, Eugene Louis Faccuito (Luigi), and Gus Giordano developing codified techniques and styles for stage and screen. Jack Cole integrated elements from vaudeville, striptease, and nightclubs, influencing generations of dancers. Bob Fosse revolutionized jazz with his distinctive, suggestive movements seen in musicals such as Cabaret and Chicago. Katherine Dunham introduced isolations and anthropological perspectives, enriching the dance’s vocabulary.

Jazz dance technique emphasizes torso mobility, parallel foot positioning (contrasting ballet’s turned-out feet), and grounded, floor-based steps. Flexibility, contractions, and isolations are key, especially in modern jazz styles. The dance incorporates syncopation, individual expression, and improvisation, reflecting its musical roots. Styles today range from Broadway jazz, which blends ballet and contemporary dance, to commercial jazz influenced by hip hop and pop music, often featuring acrobatic tricks and sharp, aggressive movements. Latin jazz, popularized by Maria Torres, emphasizes hip movement and isolations.

Jazz dance remains a living tradition practiced worldwide, taught in studios and schools. Its evolution from African American vernacular social dance to a theatrical and commercial art form illustrates a rich cultural trajectory shaped by social history, music, and individual creativity.

classical-indian-dance.name: Classical Indian dance
classical-indian-dance.era: Theoretical roots in the Natya Shastra (c. 200 BCE-200 CE)
classical-indian-dance.tagline: Umbrella term for India's Natya-Shastra-rooted classical dances
classical-indian-dance.profile: Indian classical dance (Shastriya Nritya) is an umbrella category, not a single dance, encompassing the codified classical dance traditions of India whose theoretical foundation is the ancient Sanskrit treatise Natya Shastra (Wikipedia). The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognizes eight classical dances - Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Kathakali, Mohiniyattam, Manipuri and Sattriya - while Encyclopaedia Britannica lists six, and some scholars add Chhau (Wikipedia). The Natya Shastra describes four regional pravrittis and the theory of rasa, bhava, mudras and the Tandava/Lasya dances (Wikipedia).
classical-indian-dance.insight: Sources differ on the count: the Sangeet Natak Akademi recognizes eight forms, Britannica describes six, and scholars such as Drid Williams add Chhau, Yakshagana and Bhagavata Mela (Wikipedia).

funana.name: Funaná
funana.tagline: Cape Verde's accordion-and-iron dance of forbidden joy
funana.profile: Funaná is a music and dance genre from Santiago island, Cape Verde, built on the diatonic accordion (gaita) with rhythm supplied by the ferrinho, a scraped iron rod (Wikipedia). It has a 2-beat rhythm at tempos from andante to vivace; as a couple dance, partners embrace with one arm and join hands with the other, marking the beat through quick, strong alternating knee flexions. It emerged among the Badiu of Santiago's rural interior, who turned a Portuguese-introduced accordion into a distinctly Cape Verdean sound.
funana.insight: Suppressed as "primitive" under Portuguese colonial rule and danced informally at village festivities, funaná surged after independence in 1975 — modernized by Bulimundo and later Ferro Gaita — and was officially classified as National Intangible Cultural Heritage via Ordinance n.º 9/2024 (April 9, 2024) by Cape Verde's Ministry of Culture (Wikipedia; Cabo Verde).

kuchipudi.name: Kuchipudi
kuchipudi.era: Roots in Natya Shastra; 10th-c inscriptions; systematized 17th c
kuchipudi.tagline: Andhra Pradesh's classical dance-drama danced on a brass plate
kuchipudi.profile: Kuchipudi is one of the eight major Indian classical dance forms, originating in the village of Kuchipudi in the Krishna district of Andhra Pradesh (Wikipedia). A dance-drama rooted in the Natya Shastra and the Vaishnavism tradition centered on Krishna, it blends fast rhythmic footwork, sculpturesque poses, expressive eyes and dramatic narrative, performed to Carnatic music (Wikipedia). A signature element is the tarangam, in which the dancer performs on the rim of a brass plate. Evidence of an older form appears in 10th-century copper inscriptions and the 15th-century Machupalli Kaifat (Wikipedia).
kuchipudi.insight: Historically performed by male Brahmin troupes (Bhagavatulu) and traditionally credited with refinement by the saint Siddhendra Yogi, Kuchipudi is recognized among the classical dance forms by the Sangeet Natak Akademi (Cultural India).

sattriya.name: Sattriya
sattriya.era: Created 15th-16th century by Srimanta Sankardev; classical status 2000
sattriya.profile: Sattriya (Sattriya Nritya) is a major Indian classical dance created in the 15th-16th century by the Assamese saint-scholar Srimanta Sankardev as part of Bhaona - performances of Ankiya Nat one-act plays (Wikipedia). It developed and was preserved within Sattras, the Vaishnavite monasteries of Assam, where monks performed dance-dramas on the legends of Krishna and other avatars of Vishnu drawn from texts such as the Bhagavata Purana (Wikipedia). Integrating nritta, nritya and natya, it traces its theoretical roots to the Natya Shastra and was historically performed by male monks before moving to the public stage.
sattriya.insight: The Sangeet Natak Akademi formally recognized Sattriya as one of India's classical dances on 15 November 2000, and the tradition remains a living practice of the Ekasarana Dharma communities of Assam's sattras (Wikipedia).

kecak.name: Kecak
kecak.tagline: Balinese 'monkey chant' Ramayana dance without instruments
kecak.profile: Kecak (also tari kecak) is a form of Balinese Hindu dance popularized in the 1930s, based on the Ramayana and performed primarily by men (Wikipedia). Also known as the Ramayana Monkey Chant, it is performed by a circle of as many as 150 performers wearing checked cloths who percussively chant 'cak' and move their arms, with no musical instruments. The performance depicts the battle in which the monkey-like Vanaras, led by Hanuman, help Prince Rama fight King Ravana. Kecak has roots in sanghyang, a trance-inducing exorcism ritual; in the 1930s German painter Walter Spies worked with dancer Wayan Limbak (and musician I Wayan Rindi) to develop it into a Ramayana spectacle.
kecak.insight: Scholar I Wayan Dibia argues the Balinese were already developing the cak chorus form before Spies arrived, with Limbak having incorporated baris movements into the leader's role in the 1920s (Wikipedia).

candomble.name: Candomble
candomble.tagline: Afro-Brazilian religion whose orixa worship centers on ritual dance.
candomble.profile: Candomble is an African diasporic religion developed in Brazil in the 19th century, syncretizing Yoruba, Bantu and Gbe traditions with Roman Catholicism. It venerates orixas (spirits) under a creator god, Oludumare. A central ritual involves drumming on atabaque drums, singing and dancing in a circle to invite an orixa to possess an initiate; dances embody each orixa's characteristics. Practiced in autonomous terreiros, often led by priestesses (maes de santo), concentrated in Bahia (English Wikipedia).
candomble.insight: Candomble is primarily a RELIGION, not a dance; its dances are sacred trance-inducing rituals, not performance. Per IBGE's 2022 Census, Umbanda and Candomble together had nearly 1.9 million adherents (English Wikipedia; IBGE).

calusari.name: Calusari
calusari.era: Attested from 17th-century notations (Ioan Caianu); pre-Christian roots
calusari.tagline: Romanian all-male Whitsun healing/fertility ritual dance.
calusari.profile: An all-male ritual dance from the Olt/Oltenia region of southern Romania, performed at Whitsun/Pentecost (Rusalii). Performers in white tunics with bell-trimmed hats and ribbons execute acrobatic stamping, heel-clicking, leaping and leg-swinging, carrying ornate sticks/a sword and a flag, accompanied by two violins and an accordion. Led by a vataf (master) who initiates an odd-numbered, oath-bound brotherhood; thought to confer protection, healing and fertility. Spread to northern Bulgaria (kalushari) via Romanian/Vlach settlers (English Wikipedia; UNESCO).
calusari.insight: Inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed a Masterpiece in 2005), it became Romania's first inscribed element of spiritual culture; Mircea Eliade noted its mythico-ritual scenario has nothing in common with Christianity (UNESCO; Wikipedia).

bourree.name: Bourree
bourree.era: First attested as a popular dance 1665 (Clermont-Ferrand); Baroque court form mid-17th-18th c.
bourree.tagline: Lively French folk dance of Auvergne; also a Baroque suite movement.
bourree.profile: The bourree is a French dance originating in Auvergne in the Massif Central, sometimes called the 'French clog dance,' first mentioned as a popular dance in 1665 at Clermont-Ferrand (Wikipedia; Britannica). Folk forms divide into the triple-time bourree (Montagnarde - Puy-de-Dome, Haute-Loire, Cantal, Limousin) and the duple-time line bourree (Berry, Bourbonnais, Nivernais). The step glides along the ground with stamped accents and little or no physical contact between partners - connection is through the eyes - danced in couples, quadrettes, lines or circles. Traditionally accompanied by the cabrette (Auvergnat bagpipe), vielle a roue (hurdy-gurdy), and later accordion and fiddle. As a Baroque form, Bach, Handel and Chopin wrote bourrees, giving its name to the ballet step pas de bourree (Wikipedia FR; Britannica).
bourree.insight: The folk dance and the Baroque/court form share a name and duple-time character, but no early dance notation survives to prove a direct line between the peasant dance and the courtly concert dance (Wikipedia).

kabuki.name: Kabuki
kabuki.era: Early Edo period, c. 1603 (founded by Izumo no Okuni)
kabuki.tagline: Stylized Japanese classical theatre fusing drama, music and dance
kabuki.profile: Kabuki is a classical form of Japanese theatre mixing dramatic performance with traditional dance, known for heavily stylised acting, lavish costumes and elaborate kumadori makeup (Wikipedia). It is thought to have originated in the early Edo period when Izumo no Okuni formed a female dance troupe performing in Kyoto around 1603; after women were banned in 1629 it became all-male, with onnagata specialists playing female roles (Wikipedia). Dance is integral through shosagoto dance pieces, alongside jidaimono history plays and sewamono domestic plays (Artelino). UNESCO proclaimed Kabuki a Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed it on the Representative List in 2008 (UNESCO).
kabuki.insight: Kabuki's three name-kanji read 'sing, dance and skill,' but the word actually derives from kabuku ('to lean/be out of the ordinary'), reflecting its origins among flamboyant kabukimono outsiders (Wikipedia).

pizzica.name: Pizzica
pizzica.tagline: Salento's healing dance — three forms, one driving 6/8 rhythm, revived in the 1990s as southern Italy’s cultural rebirth.
pizzica.profile: Pizzica is a popular Italian folk dance, originally from the Salento peninsula, in Apulia, and later spreading throughout the rest of Apulia and the regions of Calabria and eastern Basilicata. It is part of the larger family of tarantella.
pizzica.insight: == Notable musicians and bands == Alessandra Belloni Alla Bua Anna Cinzia Villani Antonio Castrignanò Arakne Mediterranea Canzoniere Grecanico Salentino Mascarimirì Ghetonìa Officina Zoè Enza Pagliara == Notable dancer == ALI Alice Andrea Demarco == References == == External links == Pizzica's videos Pizzica's texts La pizzica in the 1779

sega.name: Sega
sega.tagline: The Indian Ocean's foundational dance — Mauritius, Seychelles, Réunion — UNESCO-listed, hips swing, feet stay rooted.
sega.profile: Sega is one of the major music genres of Mauritius and Réunion. It is a complete performance art, involving music, story-telling and traditional dance. Musically, the most modern forms common in Mauritius are its fusion genre seggae and bhojpuri variations, whilst Réunion also features maloya, the latter being much closer to the older, typical music influences originating from Madagascar. The variety of different sega forms is reflected in the multi-ethnic populous of the indigenous population of Mauritius.
sega.insight: A particularly big turning point was his performance at the Night of the Sega at Mount Le Morne on 30 October 1964. Kaya, whose real name is Joseph Reginald Topize, was at the height of his career in 1999 when he was found dead in a prison cell.

gnawa.name: Gnawa
gnawa.era: Sub-Saharan African heritage in Morocco · UNESCO 2019
gnawa.tagline: Morocco's UNESCO-listed trance dance — Sufi brotherhoods of West African descent, iron krakebs castanets driving all-night lila ceremonies.
gnawa.profile: Gnawa music is a body of Moroccan religious songs and rhythms. Emerging in the 16th and 17th centuries, Gnawa music developed through the cultural fusion of West Africans brought to Morocco, notably the Hausa, Fulani, and Bambara peoples, whose presence and heritage are reflected in the songs and rituals.
gnawa.insight: On December 12, 2019, Gnawa was officially inscribed at UNESCO's 14th session held in Bogotá, Colombia.

cham-dance.name: Cham Dance
cham-dance.tagline: Bhutan's sacred masked Buddhist dance of merit and meditation
cham-dance.profile: The cham (Tibetan 'cham) is a masked and costumed dance of Tibetan Buddhism performed in Bhutan at Tshechu festivals, accompanied by monastic musicians on traditional instruments (Wikipedia). Dances depict incidents from the life of Padmasambhava and other saints and offer moral instruction relating to compassion; they are considered a form of meditation and an offering, performed by monks and laymen in elaborate masks and brocade robes to purify the ground and subdue evil. Tradition traces cham to the 8th century when Padmasambhava subdued local deities.
cham-dance.insight: Cham is a living sacred art rather than entertainment — a "meditation in action" in which dancers embody enlightened deities; in Bhutan its preservation is promoted by the Royal Academy of Performing Arts, and the related Drametse Ngacham (mask dance of the drums from Drametse) was proclaimed a Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in 2008.

pantsula.name: Pantsula
pantsula.tagline: South Africa's township dance — born in 1950s Soweto under apartheid, footwork low and lightning, Dickies and bucket hats.
pantsula.profile: Pantsula is a tradition and also a highly energetic dance form that originated in the black townships of South Africa during the apartheid era. It developed into a form of social commentary for black South Africans and has undergone several transformations with the country's changing political tides.
pantsula.insight: After the end of apartheid in 1994, pantsula persisted as an expression of cultural roots for many black South Africans.

lakhon-khol.name: Lakhon Khol
lakhon-khol.era: Roots in the Angkor/pre-Angkorian era; UNESCO-listed 2018
lakhon-khol.tagline: All-male Khmer masked theatre of the Reamker
lakhon-khol.profile: Lakhon Khol is a Cambodian masked dance-drama performed by men wearing elaborate painted masks, accompanied by a pinpeat orchestra and melodious recitation, enacting episodes of the Reamker (the Khmer Ramayana) with the four character types neang, neayrong, yeak (giant) and sva (monkey) (Wikipedia; UNESCO). At Wat Svay Andet near Phnom Penh it is performed for ritual purposes linked to rice farming, with spirit mediums facilitating interactions between the Neak Ta guardian spirits, performers and villagers.
lakhon-khol.insight: Lkhon Khol Wat Svay Andet was inscribed on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding on November 28, 2018 (13.COM, Port Louis, Mauritius); the tradition nearly vanished under the Khmer Rouge, surviving through a handful of masters who passed it to a new generation (Wikipedia; Bangkok Post).

pandanggo-sa-ilaw.name: Pandanggo sa Ilaw
pandanggo-sa-ilaw.tagline: The Filipino candle dance — three oil lamps balanced on head and hands, the dancer never spills a drop.
pandanggo-sa-ilaw.profile: Pandanggo sa Ilaw — the dance of light — is the most iconic of the Philippines' Spanish colonial-era folk dances, originating in Mindoro province. The dancer balances three lit tinghoy (oil lamps in coconut shells) — one on the head and one in each hand — and dances in 3/4 time, moving with such control that the flames never flicker, the oil never spills. The dance dramatises Philippine fishermen returning home from sea using lamps as signal lights, transforming a maritime practical act into a luminous national symbol.
pandanggo-sa-ilaw.insight: Pandanggo sa Ilaw is named the unofficial national dance of the Philippines by the Cultural Center of the Philippines, and it is taught in every Filipino school as part of the elementary curriculum. The three lit oil lamps — balanced on the head and two extended hands — require years of practice; advanced dancers can perform pandanggo while squatting low, spinning, and even kneeling, with the flames never flickering.

yangko.name: Yangko
yangko.tagline: Alternate romanization of Yangge, the rice-sprout folk dance
yangko.profile: Yangko is an alternate romanization of Yangge (秧歌), the traditional northern Chinese 'rice-sprout song' folk dance created by farmers in the Song dynasty to pray for harvest (Easy Tour China; English Wikipedia). The dance is smooth and compact in rhythm, with three performance types: song-and-dance duets, ground yangko and stilt yangko, using colorful theatrical-style costumes and silk handkerchiefs.
yangko.insight: As the best-known Han folk dance, Yangko/Yangge represents communal celebration, abundance and fertility and continues year-round in Chinese countryside and cities (Easy Tour China; English Wikipedia).

mongolian-tsam.name: Mongolian Tsam
mongolian-tsam.tagline: Mongolia's masked Buddhist dance — sacred lamasery ritual nearly destroyed under Soviet purges, painstakingly reborn after 1990.
mongolian-tsam.profile: Mongolian Tsam is the Vajrayana Buddhist masked ritual dance performed by lamas in Mongolian monasteries since the 16th century, derived from Tibetan Cham. Dancers wear elaborate carved-wood masks of wrathful protector deities (Yamantaka, Mahakala), dakinis, and historical Buddhist figures, performing slow choreographed sequences that exorcise harmful forces and consecrate the monastery courtyard. The tradition was nearly destroyed during the 1937 Stalinist purges that closed Mongolia's monasteries and killed thousands of lamas; today, after Mongolia's 1990 democratic transition, tsam has been painstakingly revived at Gandan, Erdene Zuu, and other restored monasteries.
mongolian-tsam.insight: Mongolian Tsam was nearly extinguished during Stalin's 1937 purges in Mongolia, when over 700 Buddhist monasteries were destroyed and 17,000+ lamas executed. The tradition survived only in fragments — a few surviving lamas memorised choreography in secret, the masks were hidden in remote homes — until the 1990 democratic transition reopened monastic life. Today the annual Tsam at Gandan Monastery in Ulaanbaatar draws Mongolians from across the country to witness the recovered tradition.

mak-yong.name: Mak Yong
mak-yong.tagline: Malaysia's UNESCO-listed all-female sacred theatre-dance — the pre-Islamic Kelantanese court tradition that survived bans and revivals.
mak-yong.profile: Mak Yong is Malaysia's ancient theatre-dance tradition, originating in the pre-Islamic Malay courts of Kelantan and Pattani over 800 years ago. Performed almost entirely by women — including the male roles — the form combines dance, drama, singing, ritual invocation, and instrumental music in stylised retellings of ancient Malay royal stories. Banned in Malaysia's Kelantan state from 1991 to 2018 for being too animist/pre-Islamic, Mak Yong survived through diaspora communities in Pattani (southern Thailand) and Singapore, returning home after restrictions eased. UNESCO inscribed Mak Yong on the Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2005.
mak-yong.insight: UNESCO inscribed Mak Yong on the Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2005 — three years before Malaysia's Kelantan state began considering lifting its 27-year ban on public performance. Today the tradition is being revived through state-supported troupes at Universiti Malaysia Kelantan and the Malaysian Arts Academy, while Pattani-based Thai-Malay communities maintained the unbroken lineage through the ban years.

adowa.name: Adowa
adowa.era: Pre-colonial Asante kingdom (origins commonly placed c. 18th century)
adowa.tagline: Akan funerary and ceremonial dance imitating the royal antelope
adowa.profile: Adowa is the most widespread social and funerary dance of the Akan, especially the Asante, of Ghana and parts of Cote d'Ivoire (Royal Museum for Central Africa). Oral tradition holds it imitates the movements of the royal antelope (adowa in Twi), said to have been sacrificed to heal an Asante queen mother. Ensembles are led by middle-aged women singers and a chorus; dancers communicate through symbolic hand gestures accentuated by a white cloth, accompanied by atumpan talking drums, apentemma, petia, and the dawuro/atoke bells (IJHSS academic study; MoTCCA).
adowa.insight: Ethnomusicologist J.H. Kwabena Nketia distinguished the forest-belt Adowa (drum-ensemble) from its coastal Fante counterpart Adzewa, accompanied by gourd rattles and a single drum (IJHSS, 2014).

tinku.name: Tinku
tinku.tagline: Bolivia's Andean ritual combat dance — Quechua and Aymara communities meet to fight as offering to Pachamama, blood as fertiliser for the earth.
tinku.profile: Tinku is a Bolivian Quechua tradition from Norte Potosí which began as a form of ritualistic combat. In the Quechua language, it means "meeting-encounter". During this ritual, men and women from different communities will meet and begin the festivities by dancing.
tinku.insight: The ritual tinku of Macha, Potosí — held every first weekend of May — remains one of the few surviving pre-Columbian Andean rituals where actual combat takes place: dancers from rival ayllu villages still engage in fist-fights that occasionally result in serious injury. The Bolivian state recognises tinku as protected cultural heritage and provides medical support during the ritual, while choreographed versions are performed at folkloric festivals across Bolivia, Peru, Argentina, and Chile.

sasa.name: Sasa
sasa.tagline: Samoa's seated group dance — rows of dancers slapping bodies, thighs, and ground in unison, faster and faster until the climax.
sasa.profile: Sasa, also spelled sāsā, is a type of folk dance from Samoa. Sasa is performed by all ages and genders, usually in groups and while seated. The word "sāsā" literally means "to strike", and is characterized by precise, rhythmic claps and intricate hand movements.
sasa.insight: A dance by the name of sasa is first mentioned in the academic literature in Buck's field notes from 1927-28, but his descriptions more closely resemble a different Samoan dance, usually referred to as siva lapalapa.

coupe-decale.name: Coupe-Decale
coupe-decale.tagline: Ivorian diaspora party music of flash and footwork
coupe-decale.profile: Coupe-decale is an Ivorian popular dance-music genre that, per Wikipedia, was developed around 2001 by a group of young Ivorian club promoters and performers known as the Jet Set, led by Douk Saga, in Paris; Douk Saga's 'Sagacite' (2002) was the first hit of the genre. It draws heavily on Congolese ndombolo and Ivorian zouglou over deep bass and repetitive, percussive arrangements, with atalaku-style hype vocals. In Nouchi slang 'coupe' means to cheat and 'decale' to run off; the scene celebrated flamboyant dress and travaillement (throwing cash). Its dances reference everyday gestures and current events.
coupe-decale.insight: Born among the Ivorian diaspora during a period of civil conflict, coupe-decale became Cote d'Ivoire's definitive pop sound and spread across Africa, later shaping Afrobeats (Wikipedia; GlobalMusix).

trepak.name: Trepak
trepak.tagline: Ukraine's Cossack squat-and-kick dance — the prysiadka leap immortalised by Tchaikovsky’s Nutcracker, Russian classical ballet, and every Slavic wedding.
trepak.profile: Trepak or tropak is a traditional East Slavic folk dance . The dance is included in the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage List of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, whose form is preserved in Tacheng.
trepak.insight: The dance is included in the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage List of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, whose form is preserved in Tacheng.

_albums.title: Dances of the Peoples of Russia

highlife.name: Highlife
highlife.tagline: Ghanaian popular music genre with associated social dancing
highlife.profile: Highlife is a Ghanaian music genre that originated along the coastal cities of present-day Ghana in the 19th century, fusing traditional Akan and Ga melodic/rhythmic structures with Western instruments, jazzy horns and two-finger guitar styles (Wikipedia; Britannica). Primarily a music genre rather than a single codified dance, it is nonetheless a social dance form encouraging individual expression (MoTCCA). It diverged into dance-band and guitar-band streams; Jacob Sam's Kumasi Trio recorded the early highlife 'Yaa Amponsah' in London in June 1928, and E.T. Mensah became the 'King of Highlife' (Wikipedia).
highlife.insight: Highlife was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity at the 20th session (20.COM) in New Delhi on 10 December 2025 (file No. 02141, 'Highlife music and dance') - Ghana's first UNESCO ICH inscription (UNESCO ICH).

limbo.name: Limbo
limbo.tagline: Trinidad's iconic backbend-under-the-bar dance — born from funeral wake tradition, conquered global beach resorts worldwide.
limbo.profile: Limbo is Trinidad and Tobago's most internationally famous dance — the contortionist art of bending backwards to pass beneath a horizontal bar that is progressively lowered. Originating in the 19th century post-emancipation Trinidad as part of African-Caribbean funeral wake celebrations (some scholars trace it to the symbolic passage of souls through the underworld), limbo was popularised worldwide by Trinidadian dancer Julia Edwards in the 1950s and 1960s. Today limbo is a fixture of Caribbean cultural performance, Carnival celebrations, and global beach resort entertainment, though the form retains its serious Trinidadian roots.
limbo.insight: According to a 1956 newspaper report, the game was revived in 1944 by Edric Connor. A film, Julia and Joyce, by Trinidadian-American Sonja Dumas, was released in 2010. == World record == The world record for lowest limbo game is held by Dennis Walston, who successfully attempted a 6-inch bar in March 1991.

quadrille.name: Quadrille
quadrille.tagline: Napoleon's ballroom dance for four couples — the French square-formation that became American square dance and Caribbean creolized national dances.
quadrille.profile: The quadrille is a dance that was fashionable in late 18th- and 19th-century Europe and its colonies. The quadrille consists of a chain of four to six contredanses. Latterly the quadrille was frequently danced to a medley of opera melodies. Performed by four couples in a rectangular formation, it is related to American square dancing. The quadrille also gave rise to Cape Breton Square Dancing via American square dancing in New England.
quadrille.insight: The dance was introduced in France around 1760: originally it was a form of cotillion in which only two couples were used, but two more couples were eventually added to form the sides of a square. Reaching English high society in 1816 through Lady Jersey, the quadrille became a craze.

polonaise.name: Polonaise
polonaise.era: 16th century Polish court · National opening dance
polonaise.tagline: Poland's national processional dance — every Polish formal ball opens with the dignified 3/4 polonaise, the dance of nobility for 500 years.
polonaise.profile: The polonaise is a dance originating in Poland, and one of the five Polish national dances in 34 time. The original Polish-language name of the dance is chodzony , denoting a walking dance. The polonaise dance influenced European ballrooms, folk music and European classical music. The polonaise has a rhythm quite close to that of the Swedish semiquaver or sixteenth-note polska, and the two dances share a common origin.

soca.name: Soca
soca.tagline: Trinidad Carnival's modern soundtrack — soca dance, hips wining to driving rhythms, fueling the largest Caribbean carnival in the world.
soca.profile: Soca music, or the "soul of calypso", is a genre of music that originated in Trinidad and Tobago in the 1970s. It is considered an offshoot of calypso, with influences from Afro-Trinidadian and Indo-Trinidadian rhythms. It was created by Ras Shorty I in an effort to revive traditional calypso, the popularity of which had been declining amongst younger generations in Trinidad due to the rise in popularity of reggae from Jamaica and soul and funk from the United States. From the 1980s onward, soca has developed into a range of new styles.
soca.insight: Shorty was the first to define his music as "soca" during 1975 when his hit song "Endless Vibrations" caused musical waves on radio stations and at parties and clubs – not just in his native Trinidad and Tobago, but also in cities such as New York, Toronto and London.

calypso.name: Calypso
calypso.tagline: Trinidad's witty social commentary dance — calypsonians lampoon politicians, lovers, and scandals; couples wine and step to the steelpan rhythm.
calypso.profile: Calypso is the foundational music and dance genre of Trinidad and Tobago — born in the 19th century from enslaved African Trinidadians' use of song as veiled social commentary and resistance under the British colonial regime. The dance is partnered and earth-low, featuring relaxed hip articulations, controlled steps, and call-and-response with the calypsonian (singer). Calypso songs are renowned for their sharp wit — lampooning politicians, lovers, and scandals — and the genre produced global stars from Lord Kitchener and Mighty Sparrow to Harry Belafonte. The steelpan, invented in 1940s Trinidad, became calypso's signature instrument.
calypso.insight: Harry Belafonte's 1956 album Calypso was the first LP in music history to sell over one million copies, hitting #1 on the Billboard charts and remaining there for 31 weeks — making calypso the first 'world music' genre to break globally. The album's hit 'Day-O (The Banana Boat Song)' is a traditional Jamaican mento song re-recorded as calypso, demonstrating the genre's enormous cultural reach across the Caribbean.

chutney.name: Chutney
chutney.tagline: Indo-Caribbean dance — Trinidad's Indian indentured-labour descendants' Bhojpuri folk meets Caribbean wining, hips and hands telling the diaspora story.
chutney.profile: Chutney is the music and dance genre of Indo-Caribbean communities — particularly Trinidad and Tobago, Guyana, and Suriname — descended from the more than 500,000 South Asian indentured labourers brought by the British between 1838 and 1917. The dance combines Bhojpuri-Indian folk movements (hand mudras, hip rolls, ankle-bell footwork) with Caribbean wining, performed to chutney music's distinctive fusion of dholak/dhantal Indian percussion, harmonium, and modern soca rhythms. Major artists like Sundar Popo, Drupatee Ramgoonai, and Ravi B made chutney one of Trinidad's most distinctive genres, and the annual Chutney Soca Monarch competition is a defining moment of Trinidad Carnival season.
chutney.insight: Chutney's most controversial moment in Trinidad came in 1988 when Drupatee Ramgoonai — the first major female chutney star — released 'Lick Down Mih Nani,' an Indian-Caribbean number that scandalised the conservative Indo-Trinidadian community by openly celebrating the wining dance vocabulary. Drupatee's defiant success cleared the way for chutney's mainstream acceptance, and today the genre is a defining marker of Indo-Caribbean identity from Port of Spain to Queens, New York.

caporales.name: Caporales
caporales.tagline: Bolivia's most popular folkloric dance — choreographed in 1969, jingling bell-bottom boots, the modern Andean cultural identity dance.
caporales.profile: The Caporales is a traditional Peruvian and Bolivian dance originated in Los Yungas of La Paz. Caporales were created and presented to the public for the first time in 1969 by the Estrada Pacheco brothers, who were inspired in the character of the 'Caporal' who is the overseer of the black slaves and was usually mixed race, wore boots and held a whip, a dance that belongs to the region of the Yungas, Bolivia. The dance, however, has a prominent religious aspect. One supposedly dances for the Virgin of Socavón and promises to dance for three years of one's life.
caporales.insight: == References == https://web.archive.org/web/20111224195130/http://www.sharingbolivia.com/2008/03/bolivian-folkloric-dances-caporales.html Archived 2016-10-06 at the Wayback Machine

saya.name: Saya
saya.tagline: Bolivia's Afro-Andean dance — the Yungas mountain communities' polyrhythmic tradition, hidden for 400 years, now reclaiming national stages.
saya.profile: Saya is the foundational music and dance of the Afro-Bolivian community of the Yungas — the descendants of enslaved Africans brought to Bolivia's silver mines starting in the 16th century, who eventually settled in the cloud-forest valleys north of La Paz. The dance is polyrhythmic and call-and-response, performed by men and women in distinct rows to the deep beat of the caja (drum), guancha (scraper), and accompanying call-singer. Long marginalized within Bolivian national folklore, saya has gained increasing visibility since the 1980s as the Afro-Bolivian community has organized around cultural recognition.
saya.insight: Bolivia's 2009 constitution — the first Andean constitution to formally recognize Afro-Bolivian identity as one of the country's founding peoples — was signed alongside national tributes to saya as a cultural heritage of the Bolivian state. Today the Yungas town of Tocaña hosts an annual Festival of Saya, and the dance is performed at every major Bolivian national celebration alongside the formerly more dominant Andean folkloric forms.

jota.name: Jota
jota.tagline: Spain's most widely danced regional folk dance — Aragonese in origin, performed across Spain in dozens of regional variants, castanets clicking, arms raised high.
jota.profile: The jota is a genre of music and the associated dance known throughout Spain, most likely originating in either Aragon or the Valencian Community. It varies by region, having a characteristic form in Aragon , Mallorca, Catalonia, León, Castile, Navarre, Cantabria, Asturias, Galicia, La Rioja, Murcia and Eastern Andalusia. Being a visual representation, the jota is danced and sung accompanied by castanets, and the interpreters tend to wear regional costumes. In Valencia, the jota was once danced during interment ceremonies.
jota.insight: Two jotas collected by Sidney Robertson Cowell for the WPA California Folk Music Project in 1939 were played by bands of different national origins: one was Mexican American, the other Portuguese American.

muineira.name: Muiñeira
muineira.tagline: Galicia's Celtic bagpipe dance — the gaita driving 6/8 footwork in northwestern Spain, the Atlantic cousin of Irish and Scottish jigs.
muineira.profile: The muiñeira is a traditional dance and musical genre of Galicia and some parts of Asturias . It is distinguished mainly by its expressive and lively tempo, played usually in 68, although some variants are performed in other time signatures. There are also variant types of muiñeira which remain in the tempo of 68 but which displace the accent in different ways. Muiñeira is associated with traditional choreographic schemes and the associated instrumentation is a form of bagpipe known as a gaita.
muineira.insight: Galician muiñeira and Irish jigs are not just rhythmically similar — they share a documented genealogical relationship. Galicia was the destination port of the medieval Camino de Santiago pilgrimage that drew Irish, Welsh, Scottish, and Breton pilgrims for over a millennium; the resulting cultural exchange embedded shared Celtic dance vocabularies in both communities. Today the World Pipe Band Championship in Glasgow regularly features Galician gaita ensembles alongside Highland pipe bands.

morris-dance.name: Morris Dance
morris-dance.tagline: England's bell-jingling village ritual dance — handkerchiefs, sticks, white clothes, blackened faces, bells at the knees; the spring fertility tradition that refuses to die.
morris-dance.profile: Morris dance is the centuries-old ritual folk dance of the English villages — earliest written records date to the 15th century — performed by costumed troupes (sides) wearing white shirts and trousers with bells strapped to their shins. Dancers move in formation around a leader, sometimes carrying handkerchiefs to wave, sometimes striking wooden sticks together in synchronized patterns. Multiple regional traditions survive: Cotswold morris (the most familiar), Border morris (darker, more theatrical), Long Sword and Rapper morris (with metal swords), and the women's Northwest morris from Lancashire. Morris is performed each May 1st (May Day) by surviving sides across England.
morris-dance.insight: Morris dancing has been performed continuously in some English villages for over 500 years — the Bampton Morris in Oxfordshire claims an unbroken tradition since the 1500s, danced every Whit Monday since records began. The English Folk Dance and Song Society (founded by Cecil Sharp in 1911) saved morris from extinction in the early 20th century by documenting every surviving village tradition; today around 800 morris sides perform across England, the United States, and Australia.

maypole.name: Maypole Dance
maypole.tagline: The Northern European spring rite — dancers weave coloured ribbons around the maypole, an unbroken pre-Christian ritual now embraced from Stockholm to Wellington.
maypole.profile: The maypole dance is the pre-Christian Northern European spring ritual where dancers — each holding a coloured ribbon attached to the top of a tall pole — weave in and out of formation in opposite directions, braiding the ribbons into geometric patterns down the pole's length. The tradition is most strongly maintained in Sweden (where Midsummer's Eve in late June is the national high holiday and the maypole — majstång — is raised in every village), Germany, England, and the Czech Republic. The maypole survives wherever Northern European descendants settled — the German diaspora in Texas, the English in Australia and New Zealand, the Swedes in Minnesota.
maypole.insight: Sweden's Midsommarafton — Midsummer's Eve — is the country's most widely celebrated national holiday, when virtually every Swedish village raises its majstång (maypole) and the population dances the small frogs dance (Små Grodorna) around it. The combination of summer-solstice daylight (the sun barely sets in central Sweden in late June) and centuries-old ritual makes Swedish Midsummer one of the most photographed traditional celebrations in Europe.

kalbelia.name: Kalbelia
kalbelia.tagline: Rajasthani snake-charmer community's serpentine women's dance
kalbelia.profile: Kalbelia is the song-and-dance tradition of the Kalbelia (Kabeliya) community of Rajasthan, formerly professional snake handlers (UNESCO). Women in flowing black skirts dance and swirl, replicating the movements of a serpent, while men accompany on the khanjari percussion and the poongi, a woodwind traditionally used to charm snakes (UNESCO). Dancers wear traditional tattoos, jewellery and garments embroidered with mirrors and silver thread; songs convey mythological stories and are improvised, transmitted orally without written texts (UNESCO).
kalbelia.insight: Kalbelia folk songs and dances of Rajasthan were inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010, and dancer Gulabo Sapera is among its best-known exponents (UNESCO/Indian Culture).
