sarandunga.name: Sarandunga
sarandunga.era: Colonial-era cofradia roots; annual feast of St John the Baptist (late June)
sarandunga.tagline: Bani's Afro-Dominican drum-dance devotion to St. John the Baptist.
sarandunga.profile: The Sarandunga is a three-part complex of Afro-Dominican music and dance performed by the cofradia (brotherhood) of San Juan Bautista in and near Bani for the saint's late-June feast. The ensemble is unusual: three small double-headed laced-goatskin drums plus one guira, mostly in lively 6/8 - unlike the long-drum palos of the wider region. Subgenres include capitana, jacana and bomba rhythms, plus the morano (sung in quatrains, played in procession and at the altar). The festival climaxes before dawn with a procession of banner, saint and drums to the Bani River, where St. John's red banner blesses the water. The dance follows the baile de palos pattern but the male role is far more virtuosic, twirling a red handkerchief (Bloomsbury Music and Sound; Lameca).
sarandunga.insight: Per the Lameca ethnographic study, the morano appears to represent a syncretism between the ancient Canary Island drum dance (tajaraste) and Central-African influences, and the community preserves Sarandunga without help from folklorists or outside cultural groups.

sanjuanito.name: Sanjuanito
sanjuanito.era: Pre-Hispanic roots asserted; popularized from early 20th c. (origins contested)
sanjuanito.tagline: Festive Andean 2/4 dance-genre, an Ecuadorian national music.
sanjuanito.profile: Sanjuanito is an Indigenous and mestizo festive dance and music genre of the Ecuadorian Sierra, originating in Imbabura Province and associated with (though not exclusive to) the Otavalo people (English Wikipedia). Written in 2/4 with pentatonic melodies in minor mode, it is tied to the Fiestas de San Juan (24 June), coinciding with Inti Raymi. Indigenous versions feature dancers circling central musicians playing two flutes and a bombo; mestizo and Pan-Andean versions add guitar, rondador, bandolin, violin, accordion and quena (EcuadorUniversitario; La Hora).
sanjuanito.insight: Considered an Ecuadorian national rhythm, it should not be confused with the Colombian 'sanjuanero,' a distinct bambuco song from Huila (Q7418595). Ecuador's FUNPAE has petitioned the Ministry of Culture and INPC for national heritage status (English Wikipedia; La Hora).

festejo.name: Festejo
festejo.profile: Afro-Peruvian festive music-and-dance developed by enslaved West Africans; no musical example predates 1800 and the modern form is a mid-20th-c. reconstruction — original choreography largely lost by ~1900, standardized from 1949 with revival by José Durand, Porfirio Vásquez and Nicomedes & Victoria Santa Cruz. Dual music+dance.

kumina.name: Kumina
kumina.profile: Afro-Jamaican Kongo-derived religion, dance and drumming complex, developed mid–late 19th c. among Central African indentured laborers after Emancipation; counterclockwise circle dance around drummers can induce possession (myal). NOT UNESCO (only Moore Town Maroon heritage 00053). Sacred = ethnographic record.

bruckins.name: Bruckins
bruckins.tagline: A stately, dipping-gliding Jamaican Emancipation pageant in royal costume.
bruckins.profile: Bruckins, also spelled brukins, is a Jamaican dance performed primarily to celebrate Emancipation Day. The dance is described as a "stately, dipping-gliding" form that may be derived from the Pavane. Its music incorporates both European and African elements. Participants accompany the dance with an elaborate pageant, dressing as European royalty, courtiers, pages, and soldiers.
bruckins.insight: Performed to celebrate Emancipation, dancers dress as European royalty in an elaborate pageant blending European and African musical elements.
bruckins.profile_long:
Bruckins, also spelled brukins, is a Jamaican dance performed primarily to celebrate Emancipation Day. Historical accounts of its origin vary; Sabine Sörgel states that the first Bruckins was celebrated in 1834 after the formal abolition of slavery, whereas Olive Lewin states that it was first celebrated in 1839 following the elimination of the apprenticeship system. The dance is characterized as a "stately, dipping-gliding" movement and may be derived from the Pavane.

The performance is accompanied by an elaborate pageant where participants dress as European royalty and members of the royal court, including courtiers, pages, and soldiers. Musically, the dance incorporates both European and African elements. Because the available sources are extremely thin, detailed documentation regarding footwork, instrumentation, and regional variants remains limited.

xoe-thai.name: Xòe Thái (Art of Xòe dance)
xoe-thai.profile: Xòe (meaning "dance" in Thái) performed at rituals, weddings and festivals in three types — ritual, circle and presentational; circle xòe (vòng xòe), dancers joining hands in synchrony, is most popular. Accompanied by gourd lutes, drums, gongs, cymbals and reed flutes. UNESCO 2021 (Vietnam’s 14th ICH element).

fakanau.name: Fakanau
fakanau.profile: Fakanau (meaning "spells") is a traditional Tuvaluan male dance-song from Niutao and Nukufetau, performed seated or standing without moving from the spot, the story told through arm and upper-body gestures while an elder kept time at the circle’s center. Composed to praise an aliki or toa and to celebrate canoe-building and fishing, it was condemned as erotic and suppressed after Samoan London Missionary Society missionaries arrived from the 1860s, disappearing until its 1960 revival by ethnomusicologist Gerd Koch.
fakanau.insight: Gerd Koch revived a fakanau on Niutao in 1960; it "became a rage, like pop music" and was filmed in 16mm that October. (Wikipedia, Fakanau)

fakaseasea.name: Fakaseasea
fakaseasea.tagline: The slow praise-song dance of Tuvalu.
fakaseasea.profile: Fakaseasea is a slow traditional Tuvaluan dance-song, historically performed mainly by young women standing and moving arms, hands and upper body while singers beat time on a slit drum or tea chest. Distinguished by very loose rules and island-specific variations, it was composed in praise of an aliki or toa and to honor canoe-building, house construction and fishing. Unlike the fakanau and oga, which died out, the fakaseasea survived, though now performed chiefly by elders for celebratory and remembrance occasions.
fakaseasea.insight: The Tuvaluan funeral tradition kupu is described as similar to fakaseasea, linking the form to mourning practice. (Wikipedia, Music of Tuvalu)

jebwa.name: Jebwa
jebwa.profile: The jebwa (also jobwa) is a Marshallese men’s stick dance in which performers carry staffs struck together as part of the choreography, traditionally accompanied by women’s aje (hourglass drum) ensembles and vocal chants. Performed only on special occasions and requiring the permission of the iroojlaplap (paramount chief), it involves selected families; accounts cite 16 dancers in coconut-leaf skirts and garlands. Distinct from the Spanish-influenced beet line dance.
jebwa.insight: The Met Museum notes Marshallese aje drums "formerly were used almost exclusively by women," accompanying the men’s jebwa — a reversal of typical gendered drumming.

sofa-dance.name: Sofa
sofa-dance.profile: Sofa is a traditional Mandinka warrior dance named for the sofa — the slave-soldiers and cavalry guardians of the Mali Empire and later Bamana and Wassoulou states. Documented by Ofosuwa M. Abiola in History Dances (Routledge, 2019), the dance encodes history through movement; Abiola situates Sofa within Mandinka cultural decolonization, tied to Fodeba Keita and Sekou Toure’s nationalist project. Performed within the Mande drum tradition led by the sabaro/kutiro ensemble.
sofa-dance.insight: Abiola’s History Dances (2019) argues such dances "can be used as an African-derived primary source for writing African history." (Routledge)

qasemabadi.name: Qasemabadi
qasemabadi.tagline: Colorful Gilaki women's rice-harvest dance from northern Iran
qasemabadi.profile: Qasemabadi (Qasem-abadi, also Ghasem Abadi) is a Gilaki chain/group dance from Qasem Abad village in eastern Gilan province on Iran's Caspian coast, performed mainly by women in vivid local costume - pleated shaliteh skirts, sequined vests, headbands and lace scarves (visitiran.ir). It is tied to the rice-growing cycle and danced in three stages symbolizing planting, tending (had) and harvesting, beginning with a prayer of thanks and moving through rapid rotations in a large circle to slower turns in tighter circles (sorin.ee). Dancers sometimes click small cups (das-sanj) between their fingers to set the rhythm (Iran's Traditional Dance, OrientTrips).
qasemabadi.insight: The dance mirrors Gilan's swampy rice-farming livelihood, with sowing, harvesting and winnowing of grain depicted through pantomime (Iranian dance, Wikipedia).

logari.name: Logari
logari.tagline: Logar Valley's freeze-and-go dance of surprise stops
logari.profile: Logari is a regional style of Afghan dance (and Attan variant) from Logar Province, the area south of Kabul famed for its skilled performers. Its signature is tricky, surprise stops in the music during which dancers freeze in a pose, holding until the music suddenly resumes; it is danced to a 7/8 meter known as Tal-e Moghuli, accompanied by rebab, tambur, dilruba, dhol and harmonium (Society of Folk Dance Historians; Folk Dance Federation of California). As an Attan style it features the trademark spins, twists and central claps.
logari.insight: The Society of Folk Dance Historians records that "the traditional style of Logar... is characterized by tricky stops in the music during which the dancers must freeze," preserving a distinctive regional aesthetic from a province long celebrated for its musicians and dancers.

sakela-sili.name: Sakela Sili
sakela-sili.profile: Sakela Sili is the ritual circle dance of the Kirat Rai (Khambu) of eastern Nepal, performed during the biannual Sakela/Sakewa festivals — Ubhauli (spring) and Udhauli (autumn). "Sili" means steps; dancers move in a circle led by a Silimangpa and Silimangma, mimicking birds and animals and depicting agricultural cycles to Sili kane drums and cymbals. Rooted in the oral Mundhum scripture and nature worship; revitalized as ethnic-identity practice from 1981. Indigenous form — ethnographic record.
sakela-sili.insight: Ethnographer Martin Wettstein notes a diaspora YouTube-driven "rising trend" of Sakela, with "dance" only a loose translation of an embodied way of moving. (Routledge, 2019)

danza-de-tijeras.name: Danza de Tijeras
danza-de-tijeras.profile: The Danza de las tijeras (Quechua: Supaypa wasin tusuq) is a competitive ritual dance of Chanka origin from Peru’s south-central Andes. Each danzaq wields polished iron rods resembling scissors blades, forming a cuadrilla with violinist and harpist; two or more cuadrillas face off in an atipanakuy duel of step-dancing and acrobatics. Danzaq descend from tusuq laykas (pre-Hispanic priests) persecuted in the colony as "supaypa waman"; while costumed, dancers are barred from churches. UNESCO-inscribed 2010.
danza-de-tijeras.insight: UNESCO element 00391: "The competition or atipanakuy may last up to ten hours... physical ability, quality of the instruments, and expertise of the accompanying musicians, are all evaluated."

itik-itik.name: Itik-Itik
itik-itik.profile: Itik-itik is a mimetic Philippine folk dance based on the movements of the itik (duck), originating in Cantilan, Surigao del Sur and documented by National Artist Francisca Reyes-Aquino. Folklore traces it to a dancer named Kanang who, performing the Sibay at a baptism, improvised short choppy steps imitating ducks splashing water; spectators imitated her and it spread. Derived from the Sibay bird dance; performed to rondalla music, men in barong tagalog, women in baro’t saya.
itik-itik.insight: A 2019 movement analysis found Itik-itik engages shoulders, hips, knees and deltoids with precise heel-toe patterns — "technique is subtle, not absent." (Asian Journal of Interdisciplinary Research)

robam-trot.name: Robam Trot
robam-trot.profile: Trot (Robam Trot) is a Khmer folk procession-dance performed at Khmer New Year to drive off the previous year’s bad luck. A traveling pantomime of a deer hunt, it stages the killing of a deer among ~16 characters (deer, hunter, giants, clowning Kanhche, drummers). "Trot" derives from Sanskrit "to cut off," referencing cutting the old year. Rooted in the Samre ethnic group’s pre-Indian animist tradition; eradicated under the Khmer Rouge and revived through state cultural efforts.
robam-trot.insight: Ethnologist Éveline Porée-Maspero recorded that by 1936 the trot procession had been abandoned in some Siem Reap villages — showing how close it came to loss. (Wikipedia)

montenegrin-oro.name: Montenegrin Oro
montenegrin-oro.profile: Crnogorsko oro is the Montenegrin national folk dance of the Dinaric Western Balkans; "oro" derives from "orao" (eagle), referencing dancers’ eagle-like movements. Young men and women form a singing circle while a man enters to dance like an eagle, joined by a woman; the gallery praises or mocks the performers. Performed without instruments (singing only), it characteristically ends with men forming a two-story human circle by standing on each other’s shoulders. Variants: Crmničko, Zetsko, Katunsko, Riječko.
montenegrin-oro.insight: Ethnochoreologist Davor Sedlarević led revitalization of 30+ rural dances; 14 (incl. oro variants) were declared national intangible heritage in 2016.

fatele.profile_long: The fatele, also known as faatele, is a traditional dance-song originating from Tuvalu and shared with the music of Tokelau. Historically, the dance was performed in a sitting or kneeling position by five or six young unmarried women who moved their arms, hands, and upper bodies while singing. The men and married women acted as the chorus. This traditional form was deeply connected to spiritual purposes and indigenous religious activity. Following the arrival of Samoan missionaries sent by the London Missionary Society in the 1860s, many traditional songs and dances were suppressed, as the rhythmic swaying was often perceived as erotic by the missionaries. As missionary influence waned in the 20th century, the Samoan siva dance tradition became popular, significantly shaping the development of the modern fatele. The modern fatele is performed at community events, church festivals, and weddings, and is used to celebrate leaders and prominent individuals. In this contemporary form, women dance in lines while standing, while men sit facing them, beating the time with their hands on floor mats or wooden boxes, such as tea chests or empty cabin cracker cans. The performance is competitive, with each island often divided into two sides. The music begins with older men singing a song in a meeting hall, known as a maneapa. The song is then gradually repeated, becoming louder and quicker as others join in, until the music reaches a climax and ends abruptly. The dancers enact the story being retold through their movements. Performers wear traditional attire, including the titi fakamanumanu (coconut leaf skirt) and the titi kaulama, which is a traditional skirt placed upon another. Tops known as teuga saka, along with headbands, armbands, and wristbands, are also standard. The modern Tuvaluan style is often described as a musical microcosm of Polynesia, where contemporary and older styles coexist.

suahongi.name: Suahongi
suahongi.tagline: Men's half-hour ritual, circle then lines.
suahongi.profile: Bellona (Mungiki) ritual sung-dance after the manga’e harvest; banned by missionaries 1940s, revived 1974.
suahongi.profile_long:
Suahongi is a significant ritual dance form originating from the Bellonese tradition of Bellona (Mungiki) Island in the Solomon Islands. The name 'Suahongi' translates to 'a circle' or 'to hover about,' reflecting the movement patterns of the dance's initial phase. Historically, the dance was an integral part of the manga'e ceremony, a ritualized sharing of surplus fish and garden crops that served as a social and economic anchor for the community. During the 1940s, the dance, along with other traditional musical expressions on Bellona and Rennell (Munggava), was banned by Christian missionaries. It remained dormant until 1974, when it was revived and documented in Honiara, largely through the efforts of Jane Mink Rossen.

The dance is performed exclusively by men and lasts for approximately half an hour. It is structured into three distinct parts. The first part, known as the buatanga, is performed in a circular formation. The subsequent two parts shift the spatial arrangement into lines. The performance is accompanied by highly rhythmic, call-and-response speech-songs that serve as an oral repository for the history of Bellona. Musicological analysis by Jane Mink Rossen describes the auditory experience as 'coordinate polyphony,' where two separate songs are rendered simultaneously to create a complex, layered soundscape. While the dance is a formal ritual, its revival has allowed for the preservation of specific Bellonese cultural narratives that were nearly lost during the mid-20th century. Today, it stands as a testament to the resilience of Bellonese tradition, distinct from the contemporary 'freestyle' dance trends currently popular among the youth in Solomon Island urban centers.

phathisi.name: Phathisi
phathisi.tagline: Bakwena leg-rattle dance with pegged, short trousers
phathisi.profile: Phathisi is a traditional dance of the Bakwena tribe of Botswana, characterized by men dancing with the lower legs of the trousers tied off with a peg (or short animal-skin pants called tshega) and by vigorous, fast footwork with leg rattles (KnowBotswana; Setapa/Wikipedia). It is one of the principal Tswana dance styles alongside setapa and borankana, performed to a lead singer and chorus with handclaps, foot-stamping and ankle rattles in a brisk compound meter.
phathisi.insight: Phathisi's distinctive pegged-trouser style was influential enough to be borrowed by neighboring traditions — the Bangwaketse incorporated it as "Setapa sa phathisi" — showing how Tswana dance forms circulated and blended across tribal boundaries in Botswana (Setapa, Wikipedia).

sammi.profile_long:
Sammi is a traditional dance form originating from the tribal communities of the Punjab region. The dance finds its roots in the Sandalbar area, though it has gained popularity across various Bars and the Pothohar regions of Pakistani Punjab. The dance is named after a young heroine of a legend, Sammi, who was described as being madly in love and who used to sing and dance as best as she could for the sake of her love. 

Performance of the dance is communal, typically structured in a circle, similar to the Giddha dance. Dancers stand in a ring and perform a specific arm movement, swinging their hands from the sides to meet in front of the body. The music is characterized by the refrain of the most popular Sammi song, "Sammi Meri waar."

The costume associated with the dance is vibrant and distinct. Dancers wear bright colored kurtas paired with full, flowing skirts known as Ghagra or Lehenga. A peculiar silver hair ornament is also associated with this dance, serving as a key visual element of the performer's attire. While the dance is a recognized part of the Punjabi folk tradition, specific technical details regarding footwork, tempo, or instrumentation beyond the vocal refrain are not described in the available sources.

bidesia.name: Bidesia
bidesia.tagline: Bhojpuri folk theatre of migration by Bhikhari Thakur
bidesia.profile: Bidesia is a popular Bhojpuri folk-theatre form of Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh that fuses dance, drama, music and song, founded by playwright-performer Bhikhari Thakur (1887-1971), the 'Shakespeare of Bhojpuri' (Wikipedia; The Theatre Times). Named after his 1917 play 'Bidesia', it dramatizes colonial-era out-migration of labourers to Bengal and Assam and the suffering of the women left behind, addressing caste, dowry and gender injustice. Male actors play female roles using the launda naach style; instruments include dholak, harmonium, tabla, jhal and bansi, drawing on Bhojpuri song genres like biraha, purbi and kajari (Wikipedia; IJELTS).
bidesia.insight: During 2009-2011 fieldwork in Patna, Vaishali and Nalanda districts, scholars estimated more than 200 active Bidesiya troupes still performing, showing the form's persistence as a vehicle of subaltern social commentary (Academia.edu).

sekete.name: Sekete
sekete.tagline: Saramaka social dance to apinti drums.
sekete.profile: Saramaka Maroon Winti-linked song-and-dance; ankle rattles and kwakwa.
sekete.profile_long: Sekete is a dance tradition practiced by the Saramaka Maroon community in Suriname, an Afro-Surinamese group descended from escaped enslaved Africans who established independent tribes in the rainforest. Rooted in the Winti religion, which blends West African spiritual practices with Christian and indigenous influences, Sekete is both a social and ritual expression. The dance involves the use of ankle rattles, known locally as kwakwa, which the dancers shake rhythmically to accompany the apinti drums. These drums provide the distinctive beat that guides the dancers' movements. Sekete is one of several original Winti dances, alongside others like awasa and songé among the Aukan Maroons. The dance is characterized by bending knees and rhythmic shaking, embodying the playful and sometimes mischievous nature of certain Winti spirits called indji-winti. Historically, Winti dances like Sekete were performed in community gatherings and spiritual ceremonies, sometimes with permission from plantation owners during the colonial period due to their aesthetic appeal. The dance remains a vital cultural practice among the Saramaka, preserving ancestral connections and spiritual identity. While the sources do not provide detailed descriptions of the dance technique or costume, the use of ankle rattles and apinti drums is central. Sekete exemplifies the survival and adaptation of African-derived dance and spirituality in Suriname's multicultural landscape.

maglalatik.profile_long: Maglalatik is a folk dance from the Philippines performed exclusively by shirtless male dancers who wear red clothing. The dancers have coconut shell halves fastened to their exposed torsos, including above the nipples, and on vests that hold four to six additional shells. They also hold coconut shells in their hands. The dancers create complex rhythms by striking the shells on their hands against those on their bodies or those worn by other dancers, all synchronized to a fast drumbeat. This percussive clapping of shells forms the core of the dance's musical and movement identity. Maglalatik is a mock battle dance representing a fight between Moros and Christians over latik, a coconut product used in Filipino cooking, from which the dance derives its name meaning "latik-maker." The dance showcases the dancers' skill and agility, and in some Filipino Martial Arts circles, it is recognized as containing hidden trapping and boxing techniques within its choreography. The dance is a vivid cultural expression combining martial imagery, rhythmic percussion, and traditional costume elements, performed to impress audiences with dexterity and speed.

amis-harvest-dance.name: Amis harvest dance
amis-harvest-dance.tagline: Interlinked arms in an ever-open circle.
amis-harvest-dance.profile: Amis/Pangcah malikoda at the Ilisin harvest festival; age-graded circle.
amis-harvest-dance.profile_long: The Amis harvest dance is an integral part of the Ilisin Harvest Festival, celebrated by the Amis indigenous people of Taiwan, primarily in the Taitung and Hualien areas during lunar July and August. This festival marks the completion of the rice harvest, replacing the earlier millet harvest ceremonies. The dance is performed by men and women of all ages, who wear traditional festival costumes and form hand-in-hand circles around the elders seated at the center. The dance movements include walking, running, and jumping, with coastal tribes exhibiting more complex and variable steps than those in mountainous regions. Singing accompanies the dance, typically with a lead singer initiating a chorus that others follow, serving as a medium to communicate with ancestral spirits and gods. The dance also functions as a social mechanism for young Amis men and women to select partners, with girls actively joining boys they favor during the dance. Elders, who hold a respected status, observe the dance and select potential future tribe leaders through this ritual. The festival includes other important ceremonies such as the adult ceremony, which marks the transition of boys into adulthood through training and tests, including a running race. The priest, a knowledgeable figure responsible for agricultural rituals and communication with the gods, oversees the festival. The dance and festival are deeply connected to the agricultural calendar, ancestral worship, and social structure of the Amis community.

skolt-sami-quadrille.name: Skolt Sami quadrille
skolt-sami-quadrille.era: Adopted from Russia/Karelia in the later 19th c.; very popular until WWII; danced to ~1950s; revitalized from the 1970s
skolt-sami-quadrille.tagline: The Skolt Sami's emblematic set dance of Russian-Karelian origin.
skolt-sami-quadrille.profile: The Skolt Sami quadrille (kolttakatrilli) is a square/set dance of the Skolt Sami, an Orthodox Christian Sami group originally from the Petsamo region (Suonikyla) and resettled after WWII around Sevettijarvi in Inari, NE Finland (Hoppu; kolttasaamelaiset.fi). Sharing much with Karelian and Northern Russian dance culture, it reached the Skolts in the latter 19th century and was historically danced at weddings and festivities to the accordion, harmonica or singing (Hoppu; Yle). Its figures resemble the Karelian katrilli - circles, vis-a-vis, place-changes - and may include a male improvisation showing skill (ripaska). After the evacuation, the community scattered along the Sevettijarvi road, the accordions were left behind in Petsamo, and the dance nearly fell into oblivion before its revival.
skolt-sami-quadrille.insight: Petri Hoppu writes that the quadrille is the best known of the Skolts' dances and, perhaps more than any other, has become emblematic of their ethnic identity; from the 1970s the Skolts began to actively revitalize their dances, establishing a quadrille performing group in Sevettijarvi as part of a Sami cultural renaissance (Hoppu, 'Rewriting Skolt Sami Dance History').

melpa-sing-sing.name: Melpa sing-sing
melpa-sing-sing.profile: Western Highlands group sing-sing; Mount Hagen Show from 1961.
melpa-sing-sing.profile_long:
The Melpa sing-sing is a cultural performance deeply rooted in the traditions of the tribes inhabiting the fertile Wahgi Valley in the Western Highlands of Papua New Guinea. While the city of Mount Hagen was only established in the 1930s following the arrival of Western explorers, the indigenous cultures of the region have long maintained complex social and ceremonial structures. The sing-sing functions as a powerful manifestation of this heritage, bringing together thousands of participants from various tribes to celebrate their distinct identities through movement, sound, and visual display.

At the heart of the sing-sing is the Mount Hagen Cultural Show, an event that has evolved into one of the most significant cultural gatherings in the country. During this festival, typically held in August, the landscape of the city transforms as warriors and community members congregate. The visual impact of the performance is defined by the participants' appearance: bodies are often anointed with grease, faces are painted in vivid, multicolored patterns, and dancers wear exceptionally elaborate headdresses that can reach nearly a meter in height. These visual elements are not merely decorative but serve as markers of tribal affiliation and status.

The performance itself is a collective endeavor, with groups of dancers moving in unison to the steady, driving sound of traditional drums. The atmosphere is one of intense communal focus, reflecting the enduring strength of traditional beliefs and social structures in the Highlands. While the Mount Hagen Cultural Show has become a major tourist attraction, the sing-sing remains a profound expression of local pride and historical continuity. The event provides a space where the diverse tribes of the Western Highlands can maintain their cultural visibility, reinforcing the social bonds that have defined life in the Wahgi Valley for generations.

te-kaimatoa.name: Te Kaimatoa
te-kaimatoa.era: Traditional; widely practised in contemporary Kiribati
te-kaimatoa.tagline: Kiribati 'dance of strength' testing the dancers' endurance
te-kaimatoa.profile: Te Kaimatoa, literally the 'dance of strength,' is the most widely practised dance in contemporary Kiribati and is performed standing (Wikipedia: Dance in Kiribati). It tests the dancer's physical endurance to hold the arms outstretched for long periods as well as their emotional endurance; the music and rhythm are often highly emotive, and it is not uncommon to see dancers weep during performance. It can be performed by men, women and children, and is accompanied by a struck wooden box and vigorous choral singing.
te-kaimatoa.insight: Te kaimatoa exemplifies the distinctive I-Kiribati dance aesthetic of outstretched, bird-like arms and sudden head movements inspired by the frigate bird that appears on the national flag (Wikipedia).

te-buki.name: Te Buki
te-buki.era: Relatively modern within Kiribati dance history
te-buki.tagline: I-Kiribati women's hip-swaying dance in heavy skirt
te-buki.profile: Te Buki is a Kiribati dance performed only by women, originating in the northern Gilbert islands of Butaritari and Makin but danced throughout the islands (Wikipedia: Dance in Kiribati). The dancer wears a thick, heavy coconut-frond skirt (te kakoko) that can weigh up to ten kilograms (22 pounds) and is generally shin length; as in other Pacific dances such as the Tahitian hura, the buki emphasises hip movement, with the torso and shoulders kept still and the hips moving gracefully like water. A wooden box (te orobaoki) is struck as percussion during formal performances.
te-buki.insight: As one of the few dance forms exclusive to women, te buki is a vital platform for female expression in I-Kiribati society, where dancers flick the heavy skirt overhead from side to side while maintaining an appearance of effortless control (Wikipedia; Grokipedia).

mwinoghe.name: Mwinoghe
mwinoghe.tagline: Chitipa's joyous 'let us enjoy ourselves' processional dance
mwinoghe.profile: Mwinoghe is a joyous instrumental processional dance of Chitipa District in north-western Malawi, performed among the Sukwa, Ndali and Bandya communities; in the Chisukwa dialect the name means 'let us enjoy ourselves' (UNESCO ICH). Dancers line up in two rows - men on one side, women on the other - performing twisting body and elaborate foot movements with no singing, accompanied only by three drums (one large ing'ina and two smaller twana), a whistle and the leader's commands (UNESCO ICH; SDNP Malawi). It was modified from the Karonga ceremonial dance Indingala between 1953 and 1955.
mwinoghe.insight: Mwinoghe features prominently in Malawi's annual Independence celebrations and serves a unifying function across communities; UNESCO inscribed it on the Representative List in 2018 (UNESCO ICH).

indingala.name: Indingala
indingala.tagline: Northern Malawi warrior dance of the Nyakyusa and Ngonde
indingala.profile: Indingala is a traditional dance of the Nyakyusa and Ngonde peoples of Karonga and Chitipa districts in northern Malawi (and across the border in Tanzania, their earlier homeland) (SDNP Malawi). It originated as a warrior dance: 'indingala' was a special drum used to signal a chief's death, dangerous animals or an enemy attack, summoning armed men to the scene (SDNP Malawi). Today it is a peaceful, highly expressive dance for emotional release, with little singing and music supplied by three drums and whistles; dancers throw their bodies in different directions while coordinating arm and leg movements (SDNP Malawi).
indingala.insight: Indingala is the parent dance from which the joyous school dance Mwinoghe was modified between 1953 and 1955 (UNESCO; SDNP Malawi).

shexani.name: Shexani
shexani.era: Traditional (one of the older Assyrian line dances)
shexani.tagline: Bouncy two-step line dance shared by Assyrians and Kurds
shexani.profile: Sheikhani (Sexani / Shekhani) is one of the older Assyrian line dances - described as 'laid-back, albeit bouncy,' built on a two-step begun with the right foot and repeated with the left, danced with interlocked hands, the left arm bent against the back and the right arm forward against the dancer ahead (Wikipedia, Assyrian folk dance). A Folk Dance Federation source calls Sheikhani the 'national dance of the Assyrians.' It is common in Behdinan, the Kurmanji-speaking part of Iraqi Kurdistan, and is also danced by Kurdish Jews and Assyrians (The Kurdish Project), while in Kurdish music it is widely known as 'Sexani.'
shexani.insight: Ethnographic research on the Assyrian diaspora frames sheikhani as a key marker of Assyrian identity - 'where there's Assyrians, there's sheikhani' - even as its line-dance, hand-holding form is shared across Assyrian, Kurdish and Turkish wedding traditions (Cairn.info).

khorezm-lazgi.name: Khorezm Lazgi

video_stack.title: Khorezm Lazgi, Uzbekistan's UNESCO-Honored Dance
The ancient artform of Lazgi dance

khorezm-lazgi.profile_long: Khorezm Lazgi is a traditional dance and musical form hailing from the Khorezm region of Uzbekistan. The dance is defined by its progressive intensity, beginning with slow, deliberate movements that gradually accelerate into a rapid, uncontrollable rhythm. According to oral tradition, the dance mimics the process of the soul entering a human body made of clay; the music is said to be the divine force that brought the limbs to life. The performance style varies by gender, with men portraying heroic and courageous themes, while women adopt a more lyrical and humorous approach. The dance is structured in three distinct parts following a short introduction, all performed in a 6/8 meter. As the music shifts, the dancer’s movements transition from isolated finger and wrist gestures to full-body engagement, ending abruptly as the tempo reaches its peak. In 2019, UNESCO inscribed the Khorezm dance Lazgi on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The form has been modernized and popularized by figures such as Komiljon Otaniyozov, who introduced new variations and instrumental styles in the mid-20th century. Today, the dance is celebrated through various regional styles, including Qayroq, Dutor, and Surnay Lazgi, each reflecting different musical accompaniments. It remains a vital part of the cultural landscape, with festivals held in the city of Khiva and global performances showcasing its unique, energetic character.

pung-cholom.name: Pung Cholom
pung-cholom.era: Roots older; 64 choloms attributed to King Chandrakirti (19th century)
pung-cholom.tagline: Manipuri drum dance, soul of Sankirtana and Raas
pung-cholom.profile: Pung Cholom (Meitei: 'roar of the drum') is a classical Manipuri drum dance regarded as the soul of Manipuri Sankirtana music and of classical (Raas) Manipuri dance (Manipuri dance, Wikipedia). Dancers play the pung (Manipuri mridang barrel-drum) while simultaneously dancing, with acrobatic leaps, spins and intricate footwork, modulating from a soft whisper to a thunderous climax; it usually serves as a prelude to the Ras Lila within the Vaishnavite Nata Sankirtana tradition and borrows movements from Thang-Ta and the Maibi Jagoi. Costume includes a white dhoti, white turban and a folded shawl over the shoulder (EZCC; Massey).
pung-cholom.insight: King Chandrakirti Singh (r. 1849-1886) is credited with composing at least 64 pung choloms, reflecting the form's deep integration into Manipuri courtly and devotional culture (Wikipedia: Pung Cholom).

wanaragua.name: Wanaragua
wanaragua.era: Emerged 18th c. during slavery; costume/disguise origins tied to St. Vincent resistance (pre-1797)
wanaragua.tagline: Garifuna masked warrior dance of resistance, where the dancer leads the drum.
wanaragua.profile: Wanaragua (Garifuna for 'mask'; also 'Jankunu' or 'John Canoe') is a masked dance performed by men during the Christmas-New Year season, traveling house to house. Dancers wear pink/white wire masks with European features (satirizing colonial slave masters), tall crepe-paper crowns, mirrors and feathers, ribboned women's-style costumes, and cowrie/shell knee rattles, dancing to the primero and segunda drums while women sing as 'gayusas' (chorus). It is one of the few dances where the drummers follow the dancer's movements rather than the reverse (MyBelize.Net; UNICEF Belize).
wanaragua.insight: Wanaragua is the most culturally significant of Garifuna masked performances - an embodied performance of resistance and resilience commemorating ancestors (Constellations, F. Arzu Carmichael; Oliver N. Greene Jr.). It falls under the UNESCO 2001/2008 Garifuna inscription.

kpanlogo.name: Kpanlogo
kpanlogo.tagline: Ga recreational drum-dance of post-independence Accra youth
kpanlogo.profile: Kpanlogo is a recreational dance and music form originating in the early 1960s among urban Ga youth in Accra, Ghana, now performed nationwide (Wikipedia). Its music draws on older Ga traditions - gome, oge and kolomashie - using the nono (metal bell), fao (gourd rattle) and a set of kpanlogo drums in 'male', 'female' and 'master' roles. The main bell pattern matches the Cuban son clave. Credited to Otoo Lincoln, who set an Ansee folktale about three princesses to a new beat, it was briefly restricted as 'indecent' before Kwame Nkrumah approved a revised choreography in 1965 (Ghana Goods; ThisWorldMusic).
kpanlogo.insight: Ghanaian master drummer C.K. Ladzekpo described Kpanlogo as 'an urban youth dance drumming and a symbol of commitment' by young people shaping post-colonial Africa's future (GhanaRemembers).

beni-ngoma.name: Beni Ngoma
beni-ngoma.tagline: Colonial-era East African dance mimicking military brass bands
beni-ngoma.profile: Beni (also Mbeni or beni ngoma) is a competitive dance-society tradition of coastal and eastern Africa in which African performers in tunics and medals imitated European colonial military brass bands and drill, complete with officer hierarchies bearing European titles (Wikipedia: Beni (music); Ranger 1975). Originating in Swahili Mombasa in the 1890s, it spread inland through Tanganyika, Kenya, Nyasaland (Malawi), Zambia and Mozambique over some sixty years, spawning variant forms such as Mganda, Kalela and Malipenga (Ranger, Dance and Society in Eastern Africa, 1975).
beni-ngoma.insight: Filed here under Malawi but fundamentally pan-East-African; in Malawi the closely related military-mimicry dance is Malipenga (with mimed 'singing horns'), developed by King's African Rifles ex-servicemen after WWI (Wikipedia: Malipenga; SDNP Malawi).

jota-aragonesa.profile_long:
The Jota Aragonesa stands as the most prominent expression of Aragonese folklore, a dance that balances technical precision with exuberant expression. Historically, its development is tied to the Ebro Valley, where it reached its peak in the 19th century. While often associated with Aragon, the dance is a regional phenomenon found across Spain, from the Cantabrian mountains to the plains of Castile, each region imbuing the form with unique musical and choreographic nuances. The dance is fundamentally a visual representation of music, traditionally accompanied by the sharp, percussive clatter of castanets and the melodic interplay of stringed instruments like the bandurria and guitar.

At its core, the Jota is a dance of elevation. Dancers perform small, sharp leaps that contrast with the grounded nature of other Spanish folk traditions. The posture is upright and proud, with arms held high, often framing the head. The footwork, while reminiscent of the waltz in its circularity, is significantly more varied and demanding, requiring agility and stamina. In its purest social form, the Jota is a communal act of cohesion, but in the theatrical versions popularized since the late 19th century, it has become a centerpiece of zarzuelas, films, and competitive festivals. These staged versions demand high technical proficiency, with dancers executing complex patterns that reflect the pride and history of their respective regions.

The music accompanying the Jota is typically set in a 3/4 or 6/8 meter, providing a driving, rhythmic pulse that dictates the dancers' movements. The songs themselves are diverse, ranging from religious hymns and patriotic anthems to wry, humorous observations on daily life and love. This lyrical content is structured in eight-syllable quartets, a form that reinforces the dance's rhythmic structure. Whether performed in a village square or on a professional stage, the Jota remains a living tradition, continuously adapted by folkloric groups to maintain its relevance as a pillar of Spanish cultural heritage.

moreska.name: Moreska
moreska.profile: A traditional sword dance from the town of Korcula on the Adriatic island of the same name (southern Dalmatia). Two groups of male dancers (Moreskanti) - historically Moors vs Christians, later the White King vs the Black King (Moro) - stage a mock battle in seven sword-clashing figures (kolapa) over a captured maiden, the Bula. Accompanied by brass-band music with a score reconstructed by local composer Krsto Odak. Performed on St. Theodore's Day (29 July) and weekly in summer; moreskanti are documented in a Korcula town journal of 1666 (English Wikipedia; Korcula Tourist Board).
moreska.insight: Korcula is the only place where the Moreska survives with each soldier wielding two real swords, the dance having vanished elsewhere in the Mediterranean by the 19th century (English Wikipedia).

tautoga.name: Tautoga
tautoga.profile: The tautoga is considered the most formal and restrained style of Rotuman dance, performed at large festivities and ceremonies (kato'aga) on the island of Rotuma, a Polynesian-outlier dependency of Fiji since 1881 (Wikipedia). Comparable to the Tongan lakalaka and Tuvaluan fatele, it is performed by a dance group (hafa) of 10 to 100+ people arranged in rows, men on one side and women on the other. It is structured as a suite of three dance types - sua, tiap hi'i and tiap forau - accompanied by elders beating a pile of folded mats with sticks. Dancers wear the ha'fali (a sulu-like wrap), tefui garlands and a sweet-smelling flower in the ear (Wikipedia).
tautoga.insight: As the centrepiece of Rotuman kato'aga and a marker of a culture whose language is endangered, the tautoga is treated respectfully as ethnographic ceremony rather than entertainment; it remains central to Rotuman Language Week celebrations across the diaspora (PMN).

gurage-dance.name: Gurage dance
gurage-dance.tagline: Acrobatic, full-body dance of Ethiopia's Gurage
gurage-dance.profile: The Gurage dance (Guragigna) is the energetic traditional dance of the Gurage people of south-central Ethiopia. Per the Mocha Ethiopia Dance Group and Universal Tongue, it is fast-paced and athletic, demanding full-body coordination as dancers move arms and legs forward and back while jumping on alternate legs - reflecting the Gurage's reputation as hard workers; women dance in trousers with hair covered for the rapid tempo. It accompanies weddings, religious festivities and community gatherings, with music on masenqo and kebero.
gurage-dance.insight: Guragigna is among Ethiopia's most acrobatic regional dances and a vibrant marker of Gurage identity within the country's mosaic of more than 80 ethnic dance traditions (Mocha Ethiopia Dance Group; Universal Tongue).

govend.name: Govend
govend.tagline: Kurdish communal hand-holding circle dance of celebration and identity
govend.profile: Govend (also gowend, halparke, helperke, dilan) is the general Kurdish term for the communal hand-holding circle/line dance, the joyful heart of Kurdish weddings, Newroz and festivals (Kurdish dance, Wikipedia). Dancers link hands, shoulders or interlocked pinky fingers and follow a leader (sergovend/sercopi) who often waves a handkerchief, moving from slow stately steps to fast, exhilarating sequences, typically accompanied by zurna and davul/daf (The Kurdish Project; Kurdish dance, Wikipedia). It is danced across Iraqi Kurdistan and in Turkey, Syria and Iran, and is notably mixed-gender, distinguishing it from neighboring traditions; it is closely related to halay and dabke (Kurdish dance, Wikipedia).
govend.insight: In Sorani the dance is called copi (chopee), led by a sercopi - etymologically linking govend to the wider Iraqi chobi/chopi line-dance family (The Kurdish Project).

merengue-tipico.name: Merengue tipico
merengue-tipico.era: Oldest style of merengue; dates to the 1840s-1850s
merengue-tipico.tagline: The oldest, accordion-led Cibao style of merengue.
merengue-tipico.profile: Merengue tipico (also merengue cibaeno, colloquially perico ripiao) is the oldest surviving style of merengue, originating in the rural Cibao around Santiago in the mid-19th century. Early ensembles used strings, but two-row diatonic button accordions replaced them when Germans arrived in the 1880s via the tobacco trade, joined by guira, tambora and (historically) the marimba box bass, later electric bass, saxophone and congas. It is fast (2/4), with rhythms including merengue derecho and pambiche, and a climactic improvisational jaleo/mambo section - the 'country music' of the DR (English Wikipedia; Smithsonian Folkways).
merengue-tipico.insight: Per ethnomusicologist Sydney Hutchinson and Smithsonian Folkways, a strong transnational merengue tipico scene has connected Santiago and New York City since the 1960s, reshaping the tradition while keeping it alive in the diaspora.

qeej-dance.name: Qeej dance
qeej-dance.era: Centuries-old; rooted in Hmong ancestral tradition
qeej-dance.tagline: Hmong reed-organ dance that guides souls and dazzles crowds
qeej-dance.profile: The qeej (pronounced 'keng') is the Hmong free-reed bamboo mouth-organ and the acrobatic dance performed while playing it; the player spins, leaps, crouches and somersaults without interrupting the melody (Organology; Grinnell College). At Hmong New Year it is competitive entertainment, but its sacred role is at funerals, where qeej speech-surrogate melodies encode poems instructing the soul of the deceased on its journey to the ancestral realm (Falk, Asian Folklore Studies 2004). Players dance in symbolically meaningful circular movements during ceremonies (Grinnell College).
qeej-dance.insight: The qeej is the Hmong cognate of the Chinese lusheng and the Lao khaen; on English Wikipedia the instrument is covered under 'Lusheng', while German Wikipedia titles its article 'Qeej' (Wikidata Q1595537).

ura.tagline: Cook Islands drum dance that tells stories with the hips
ura.profile: The 'ura is the traditional dance of the Cook Islands (Polynesia), most famously the 'ura pa'u or drum dance set to fast, layered rhythms from a full ensemble of drums (pate, tokere, pa'u). Per Wikipedia, women move the hips, legs and hands to narrate stories of the ocean, birds, flowers, love and sadness, while men flap their knees in a semi-crouch holding the upper body steady; dancers wear pareu and kikau (grass) skirts with 'ei flower and shell garlands. It belongs to a family including Tahitian 'ote'a and Hawaiian hula.
ura.insight: 'Ura is the centrepiece of Cook Islands cultural identity, celebrated annually at the Te Mire Ura (Dancer of the Year) competition, and Cook Islanders are widely regarded among Polynesia's finest drummers and dancers (Wikipedia; Te Papa).

gumboot-dance.profile_long:
The Gumboot dance, also known as Isicathulo in Zulu, originated in the late 19th century among black miners in the gold mines of South Africa, particularly around Johannesburg and the Witwatersrand region. These miners were subjected to harsh working conditions, including being chained, working in flooded tunnels, and a strict prohibition against speaking to each other under threat of severe punishment. To communicate, they developed a coded language using rhythmic slaps on their Wellington boots (gumboots), stamping, clapping, and rattling chains. The boots were often embellished with bells or bottle caps to enhance the sound, recalling the chains that once bound them.

This percussive dance form uses the body and boots as idiophones, creating complex polyrhythms and total body articulation derived from traditional African dances. Many routines parody the movements of mine officers and guards, serving as a subtle form of resistance and social commentary. Over time, gumboot dancing moved from the mines to the surface, becoming a popular cultural and social expression among miners and their communities. It evolved into a performance art with groups competing and performing in company amphitheaters and public spaces.

Today, Gumboot dance is commonly seen in South African tourist areas such as the Victoria & Alfred Waterfront in Cape Town, performed by youth groups and professional troupes. It has also gained international recognition through music collaborations, such as Paul Simon's "Gumboots" on his album Graceland, and through folk groups like Zimbabwe's Black Umfolosi. The dance continues to evolve, incorporating modern elements while respecting its origins. Educational groups like the Gumboot Core Team at Pearson College UWC maintain the tradition authentically, and organizations like World of Step work to preserve its historical significance.

The dance's music often includes guitar, accordion, and violin accompaniment, though originally it was performed without instruments. The boots' sounds combined with body percussion create a distinctive rhythmic texture. The dance is both a cultural symbol of resilience and a vibrant artistic form, reflecting the miners' history and contemporary South African identity.

meshrep.profile: Meshrep (Uyghur: مەشرەپ; Chinese 麦西热甫) is a traditional Uyghur gathering combining poetry, muqam music, dance, games and moral adjudication, found chiefly in Xinjiang (English Wikipedia; UNESCO). Men play progressively faster muqam on the dutar while participants compete at whirling circle dances; it functions as both a 'classroom' and a 'court'. UNESCO notes all Uyghur people may participate.
meshrep.insight: Inscribed in 2010 on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding (ref 00304), Meshrep is the most important cultural carrier of Uyghur tradition (UNESCO).

The best-known form is Batang Xianzi from Batang County, Garzê, Sichuan; movements are slow and graceful, forming winding 'dragon' formations. Lyrics are poetic records of local life dating back over 1,000 years.
xianzi.insight: Batang Xianzi was inscribed in 2006 in China's first batch of national intangible cultural heritage and is called a 'living fossil' of Tibetan song and dance (CGTN).

tsamiko.name: Tsamiko
tsamiko.era: Klephtic/armatoloi tradition; iconic of the Greek War of Independence (1821-1830)
tsamiko.tagline: Mainland 3/4 men's line dance of the klephts.
tsamiko.profile: A popular mainland Greek folk dance in 3/4 meter, also called Kleftikos for its association with the klephts who fought in the War of Independence. Slow, strict tempo emphasizing 'attitude, style and grace' over steps; dancers link hands bent 90 degrees at the elbows in a line/open circle. The lead dancer performs high acrobatic leaps (scissor-like kicks) supported by the second dancer. Danced almost exclusively by men, sometimes in the fustanella; most popular in Central Greece (Roumeli), the Peloponnese, Thessaly and Epirus. Played by zournas and daouli, or clarinet, violin and laouto (English Wikipedia; Domna Samiou Association).
tsamiko.insight: The name means 'dance of the Chams' (from Tsamouria/Chameria), though musicologist Samuel Baud-Bovy noted the Greek tsamiko was not actually danced among Cham Albanians; it is performed at national commemorations of the 1821 revolution.

hasapiko.name: Hasapiko
hasapiko.era: Medieval (Byzantine-era origin as a butchers' battle mime)
hasapiko.tagline: The 'butcher's dance' of Constantinople; basis of sirtaki.
hasapiko.profile: A Greek folk dance from Constantinople, originating in the Middle Ages as a sword/battle mime by the Greek butchers' guild, adopted from the Byzantine military; historically called makellarikos horos. The slow version (hasapikos varys, 'heavy') is in 4/4; the fast version (grigoro hasapiko or hasaposerviko) in 2/4. Danced in a short line/open circle, hands on neighbours' shoulders, with synchronized steps; accompanied by bouzouki and rebetiko-era ensembles. Sirtaki is a modern choreographed version of it (English Wikipedia; Dance Museum).
hasapiko.insight: The hasapiko is the structural basis of the 1964 sirtaki; its fast, Balkan-influenced form is the hasaposerviko (English Wikipedia, citing Leontis, 'Culture and Customs of Greece').

rouf.name: Rouf

rouf.profile: Rouf (pronounced 'ruf' in villages, 'row' in towns; also Rouff) is a Kashmiri women's folk dance that welcomes spring and is also performed during Eid and Ramzan (J&K Tourism). Dancers form two parallel rows facing each other with interlocked or held hands, swaying forward and backward; its hallmark is intricate synchronised footwork (J&K Tourism). It originated within the Muslim community of the Kashmir Valley and was later embraced across the valley; women wear colourful pheran with a headscarf and traditional silver jewellery (J&K Tourism; INTACH).
rouf.insight: Rouf is performed communally on joyous occasions and traditionally marks the arrival of spring, embodying the seasonal rhythm of the valley; songs accompanying it are often interwoven with the chakri musical tradition (INTACH; Music of Jammu and Kashmir).

Revived by Mestre Popo (Paulino Aluisio de Andrade) in 1943 and spread internationally by Emilia Biancardi's Viva Bahia group (English Wikipedia; Encyclopedia.com).

danza-de-la-botella.profile_long: Danza de la Botella is a traditional folk dance from Paraguay distinguished by performers balancing glass bottles on their heads. Female dancers typically wear ankle-length skirts reminiscent of 19th-century rural Paraguayan attire. The dance likely evolved from the galopa folk dance, which involved balancing jugs on the head, with bottles replacing jugs over time. Performances are accompanied by Paraguayan polka music, a lively genre that sets the rhythm and mood. The dance is largely improvised, with basic movements involving dancers extending their arms to hold the ruffles of their skirts, creating an illusion that no bottles are balanced atop their heads. The dance can be performed individually, in pairs, or groups, with each dancer balancing one or two bottles. More skilled dancers can balance ten or more bottles stacked. The bottles are often decorated with tricolored ribbons reflecting the Paraguayan flag or adorned with flowers. When multiple bottles are stacked, they are designed to attach to each other securely but not to the dancer’s head, ensuring safety and balance. The dance has appeared in popular culture, including tasks on The Amazing Race and performances on Got Talent España, highlighting its cultural significance and visual appeal. The dance’s improvisational nature and the technical skill required to balance multiple bottles while moving to polka music make it a striking and challenging folk tradition.

tari-piring.name: Tari Piring (Plate dance)
tari-piring.era: Pre-Islamic harvest ritual origins; popularized by Huriah Adam
tari-piring.tagline: Minangkabau plate dance of whirling balanced plates
tari-piring.profile: Tari Piring (Piriang) is a traditional Minangkabau plate dance from West Sumatra, traditionally from Solok (Wikipedia; Indonesia.travel). Performed by women, men or couples, each dancer holds a plate in each hand and vigorously rotates them in fast formations without dropping them, tapping the plates with a finger ring for sonic accompaniment. It originated as a harvest fertility ritual of gratitude to the gods, in which offerings of food were carried on plates; with the arrival of Islam it became a performance dance rather than worship. Movements draw on Minangkabau silat, and it is accompanied by the talempong and saluang. Performances often end with dancers stepping barefoot on broken plate shards.
tari-piring.insight: Now performed at weddings and welcomes alongside saman, pendet and jaipong, Tari Piring has become one of Indonesia's signature dances for promoting national tourism and culture (BINUS; Indonesia Sentinel).

zapin.profile_long:
Zapin is a Malay dance tradition introduced by Arab Muslim traders and missionaries from Hadramaut, Yemen, during the 14th and 15th centuries. Initially performed exclusively by men in religious contexts, it has transformed into a secular and inclusive art form practiced by both genders across the Malay world, including Malaysia (notably Johor), Indonesia (Sumatra and Kalimantan), Brunei, and Singapore. The dance is typically performed in pairs or groups, accompanied by a traditional ensemble featuring the gambus (a short-necked lute related to the Arabic oud), marwas (small double-headed drums), rebana (frame drums), gendang (barrel drums), violin, accordion, harmonium, and gong. 

The musical performance often begins with a solo gambus improvisation called taqsim, followed by structured melodies interspersed with rhythmic drum interludes known as kopak, and concludes with a closing movement called wainab. The rhythmic patterns are complex, with interlocking drum beats creating a layered texture, and the melodies often use hexatonic or heptatonic scales. Vocals may be in Arabic or Malay, conveying moral and Islamic teachings, thus serving as a form of dakwah (religious outreach).

Movement-wise, Zapin features swift, simple footwork with minimal ornamentation, emphasizing synchrony and modesty. Johor’s Zapin Lenga style exemplifies this with six numbered steps connected by kopak transitions and a graceful closing wainab. The dance embodies Malay values of decorum, respect, and cultural harmony. Costumes reflect this cultural identity: male dancers wear traditional Baju Melayu Teluk Belanga with songkok caps, while female dancers wear modest Baju Kurung Teluk Belanga with sarongs and selendang shawls.

Zapin’s functions extend beyond entertainment to social bonding, spiritual education, and cultural diplomacy. It is performed at weddings, communal feasts, Quran completion ceremonies, and Islamic holidays. The dance’s preservation is supported by communities and cultural practitioners in Johor and beyond, and it is recognized as a living heritage. A joint nomination for UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription by Singapore, Brunei, Indonesia, and Malaysia is underway.

Numerous regional variants exist, each with distinct movement styles and musical nuances, reflecting local adaptations across the Malay Archipelago. The dance’s Arab origins remain evident in its musical instruments, rhythmic structures, and some choreographic elements, while Malay cultural values shape its aesthetic and social roles. Zapin thus represents a dynamic cultural synthesis and a continuing tradition of Malay identity and Islamic heritage.

najdi-ardah.name: Najdi Ardah
najdi-ardah.profile: Saudi Arabia's national sword dance — Najdi Ardah (Saudi Arabia, Najd). Full sourced 9-field profile in research artifact; concise schema stub pending text expansion.
najdi-ardah.image_significance: Saudi Arabia's national sword dance. A representative image shows a line or row formation, often with canes, swords or flowing veils — Najd, Saudi Arabia.
najdi-ardah.profile_long:
The Najdi Ardah, or Alardah Alnajdiyah, is a prominent folkloric performance deeply rooted in the cultural identity of Saudi Arabia. Historically, the dance served as a martial display, performed by tribal men in the central Najd region to demonstrate combat readiness and boost morale before engaging in warfare. The term 'ardah' is believed to derive from the Arabic verb 'ard', meaning 'to show' or 'to parade', reflecting its original purpose as a public exhibition of a tribe's fighting strength. Today, the practice has evolved from its martial origins into a celebratory performance held at weddings, births, graduations, and major national events. It is widely recognized as the most practiced and televised male folkloric dance in Saudi Arabia, with the government officially referring to it as 'Saudi Ardah' in the 21st century.

The performance is characterized by a structured formation where men stand in two opposing rows, leaving a space in the center. Participants, who represent all ages, professions, and social classes, are dressed in traditional attire and often carry light swords. A central figure, also in traditional costume, carries a flag around which the participants gather at the conclusion of the ceremony. The auditory landscape of the performance is defined by the interplay of drums and spoken poetry. A poet recites verses relevant to the specific occasion, which are then repeated as a refrain by the participants. The drumming follows a specific sequence, with larger drums providing the base rhythm followed by smaller drums. As the poetry and percussion progress, the participants mark the rhythm through synchronized body movements, swaying from front to back, and coordinated sword movements, lifting the blades from top to bottom.

In December 2015, the UNESCO committee meeting in Windhoek, Namibia, inscribed Alardah Alnajdiyah on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The organization noted that the dance serves as a fundamental component of the cultural expressions of the communities that practice it, promoting respect and group cohesion. While the Najdi variant is the most common, the broader ardah tradition is diverse, with distinct regional variations found in the southern provinces of Najran, Asir, and Jizan. The performance remains a male-exclusive tradition, with women’s involvement primarily focused on the creation of the costumes worn by the dancers. The dance is transmitted through schools, community organizations, and public events, ensuring its continued relevance in modern Saudi society.

ayyalah.name: Ayyalah (Al-Ayyala)
ayyalah.profile: The Gulf's victory cane-and-drum dance — Ayyalah (Al-Ayyala) (Oman/UAE, Gulf). Full sourced 9-field profile in research artifact; concise schema stub pending text expansion.
ayyalah.image_significance: The Gulf's victory cane-and-drum dance. A representative image shows a line or row formation, often with canes, swords or flowing veils — Gulf, Oman/UAE.
ayyalah.profile_long: Ayyalah, also known as Al-Yawlah or Al-Razha, is a cornerstone of the cultural heritage of the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman. Historically rooted in Bedouin tribal traditions, the dance was originally performed to celebrate victory following tribal conflicts or successful pearl diving expeditions. Today, it functions as a vital expression of national identity, solidarity, and the values of defense and peace. The performance is characterized by its martial origins, where the movements of the dancers simulate a battlefield. The structure of the dance typically involves two rows of men, often numbering around twenty in each line, facing one another. These participants carry thin bamboo sticks, which symbolize spears or swords, though in some variations, performers may use dummy rifles or actual swords. The choreography is highly synchronized, with the men moving their heads and sticks in unison to the rhythm of the drums. In the United Arab Emirates, the performance is often augmented by the presence of girls wearing traditional dresses, who stand at the front of the rows and perform the 'naash'—a ritual where they toss their long hair from side to side. This act is said to symbolize the protection of women by the warriors. The musical accompaniment is essential to the Ayyalah, consisting of large and small drums, tambourines, brass cymbals, leather bagpipes, and flutes. The melody is noted for having seven tones in an irregular, repeating pattern, which guides the movements of the dancers. The chanted poetry, which varies depending on the occasion, glorifies nomadic life and tribal virtues. The dance is inclusive, involving performers from diverse backgrounds and age groups, with the role of the lead performer often being an inherited position responsible for training others. The Ayyalah is not a static tradition; it has evolved into various regional forms, such as the Al-Harbiyya, where the chant dictates the movement, and the Al-Wahabbiyya, found in the rural and coastal areas of Ras Al-Khaimah and Fujairah, which utilizes weapons and is performed to a slower drum rhythm without the participation of women. In Oman, the dancers arrange themselves in two rows facing each other, moving forward and swaying back and forth to simulate the head of a moving camel. The significance of the Ayyalah was solidified on the international stage in November 2014, when it was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage. This recognition has bolstered efforts to preserve the dance, ensuring that the skills, values, and knowledge associated with the performance are transferred from one generation to the next. Modern adaptations have also emerged, such as the Al Meydan reality series, which introduced a competitive format similar to televised talent shows, and the annual Shaikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Championship, which keeps the tradition relevant for younger generations while maintaining its core, historical structure.

kartuli.name: Kartuli
kartuli.tagline: Georgia's lyrical, untouching wedding couple dance
kartuli.profile: Kartuli is the romantic couple or wedding dance considered the crown jewel of Georgian choreography, without strong regional markers (Wikipedia; georgia.travel). During the dance the man may not touch the woman or even her clothing and must keep a precise distance, his upper body motionless, his gaze fixed on her - expressing controlled feeling and respect; the woman keeps her eyes downcast and glides 'as a swan on the smooth surface of a lake.' Conceived as a theatrical synthesis in the 11th-12th centuries, it follows a 6/8 rhythm and unfolds in parts (invitation, duet, the woman's solo, finale) (hobbyblendfun).
kartuli.insight: Kartuli encodes the social code of the Georgian gender ideal - restraint, dignity and reverence for women - and in 2020 was designated a Monument of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Georgia (tbilisitrips).
kartuli.image_significance: Couple wedding dance; he never touches her. A representative image shows upright carriage, sweeping arm lines and embroidered dress — national, Georgia.

khevsuruli.name: Khevsuruli
khevsuruli.tagline: Khevsureti's sword-and-shield dance of love and combat
khevsuruli.profile: Khevsuruli is a mountain dance from Khevsureti combining love, courage, respect for women, competition and skill (Wikipedia; Sukhishvili). It opens with a flirting couple; a second young man appears, also seeking the woman, triggering vigorous fighting between the two men and their supporters with swords and shields. The conflict halts when a woman throws her head veil between the combatants (tradition demands they stop), only to resume once she leaves. The finale is deliberately open-ended. Highly technical, it requires intense practice to perform safely. It derives from the martial culture of the Khevsurs, highland warriors who practised the Khridoli martial art.
khevsuruli.insight: Khevsuruli is often called the best representative of the Georgian spirit, dramatizing the highland code in which a woman's veil can instantly stop armed conflict (caucasustravelguide); the Khevsurs were renowned warriors who served as royal bodyguards.
khevsuruli.image_significance: Mountain sword-and-shield duel dance. A representative image shows upright carriage, sweeping arm lines and embroidered dress — Khevsureti, Georgia.

perkhuli.name: Perkhuli
perkhuli.profile: Perkhuli is a predominantly male Georgian folk round dance; its name comes from 'pekhi' (foot) (Wikipedia). Of at least 20 versions, the 'multi-level' perkhuli is among the most popular, with one group of dancers standing on another group's shoulders to music in 3/4 time; another version alternates slow and fast rounds in 4/4. The northwestern mountain region of Svaneti is especially rich in perkhuli repertoire. Often described as the ritual forebearer of all Georgian folk choreography, it is danced with songs and shouts and welcomes participants of any number (georgia.travel).
perkhuli.insight: Perkhuli was inscribed on the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Georgia list in 2013 and is regarded as the foundational Georgian dance, its 'living towers' surviving in regional forms such as the Gurian Partsa (Wikipedia).
perkhuli.image_significance: Multi-tier round/tower dance. A representative image shows upright carriage, sweeping arm lines and embroidered dress — mountains, Georgia.

simdi.name: Simdi
simdi.tagline: Stately Ossetian mass couple dance in black and white
simdi.profile: Simdi is an Ossetian-origin folk dance performed in Georgia by many couples, distinguished by long-sleeved costumes, exceptionally high headwear and the stark contrast of black and white attire (Wikipedia; Georgia About). Its beauty lies in strict graphic line formations, softness of movement and precise synchrony; stern-looking men stand beside the women as a protective, deferential presence. Derived from the verb 'simyn' ('mass dance'), a Simd can involve very large numbers of dancers; it traces back to the Alans and originally had ritual, sacred meaning connected with a sun cult and military training (hobbyblendfun). It is closely related to, but distinct from, the Ossetian invitation dance Khonga.
simdi.insight: Simdi was historically a courtship vehicle for young people forbidden to meet alone - the long sleeves and 'no-touching' rule enforced formal propriety - and survives as a celebration of classical purity and harmony among Georgia's Ossetian community (Georgia About).
simdi.image_significance: Stately long-sleeved gliding couples. A representative image shows upright carriage, sweeping arm lines and embroidered dress — Ossetian-origin, Georgia.

shalakho.name: Shalakho
shalakho.tagline: The Caucasus' fiery competitive courtship dance
shalakho.profile: Shalakho (Շալախո) is a dynamic, acrobatic dance known throughout the Caucasus, including Armenia, Georgia and Azerbaijan. Its most common form features two or more men competing to attract a woman's attention, using swords or sticks and performing fast jumps, kicks and spins, while the woman moves with softer, shorter steps (NaTakallam; Armenian dance). It is a lively solo/competitive dance performed at public gatherings.
shalakho.insight: As a shared Caucasian dance claimed by Armenian, Georgian and Azerbaijani traditions, shalakho illustrates the deeply intertwined performance cultures of the region, even as each group maintains its own version and styling (NaTakallam).
shalakho.image_significance: Competitive men's solo showpiece. A representative image shows upright carriage, sweeping arm lines and embroidered dress — Caucasus, Armenia/Georgia.

tor-tor.name: Tor-Tor
tor-tor.era: Ancient; some accounts estimate from the 13th century
tor-tor.tagline: Batak ritual dance of stomping feet and gondang music
tor-tor.profile: Tortor (Tor-Tor) is a traditional Batak dance from North Sumatra, originally a sacred ritual dance performed at funerals, healing ceremonies and other Batak ceremonies (Wikipedia). For the Batak it carries cultural and spiritual value, expressing hopes and prayers; performance types include Tortor Sombasomba (worship), Simonangmonang (victory) and Habonaran (truth). The name comes from the sound of dancers stomping their feet on a Batak house's floorboards. It is accompanied by gondang musical instruments, with dancers wearing ulos cloth; movements are simple - hands waving up and down and feet stamping to the rhythm - and the host (hasuhutan) opens with a request to the gondang musicians.
tor-tor.insight: Tortor functions as a medium of communication: through its movements, interaction occurs between ceremony participants, with songs appealing to God and ancestral spirits for safety, prosperity and blessing (Wikipedia; Trekking Orangutan Sumatra).
tor-tor.image_significance: Batak ancestral ritual dance. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — N. Sumatra (Batak), Indonesia.

hudoq.name: Hudoq
hudoq.era: Ancestral agricultural ritual; annual Hudoq festivals continue today
hudoq.tagline: Dayak masked spirit dance for rice fertility and harvest
hudoq.profile: Hudoq is a masked agricultural spirit dance and ritual of the Dayak Bahau, Modang, Busang, Aoheng and Penihing peoples of East Kalimantan, primarily in the Mahakam Ulu region (Wikipedia; WWF). According to traditional belief the hudoqs are thirteen crop-destroying pests (rats, boars, leopards, crows), symbolized by dancers wearing carved masks and jackets of banana and areca-palm leaves. Held around September-October after rice planting, the dance invokes blessings from ancestors and gods for fertile crops and wards off pests, with dancers acting as mediums between humans and guardian spirits.
hudoq.insight: The dance has been recognized as a National Intangible Cultural Heritage by Indonesia's Ministry of Education and Culture, and the Hudoq Pekayang Festival draws hundreds of dancers from Mahakam Ulu villages (TheForestForever; WWF).
hudoq.image_significance: Masked harvest-thanksgiving of the Dayak. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — E. Kalimantan (Dayak), Indonesia.

kipas-pakarena.name: Kipas Pakarena
kipas-pakarena.era: Heritage of the Gowa Kingdom (16th-18th century)
kipas-pakarena.tagline: Graceful Makassar fan dance of the Gowa court
kipas-pakarena.profile: Kipas Pakarena is a fan dance originating from Gowa, South Sulawesi, a cultural tradition of the Makassar people dating to the Gowa Kingdom (id.Wikipedia; Indonesia-Tourism). The name combines 'pa' (the performer) and 'karena' (to play). Performed by women holding folding fans with slow, gentle movements, it depicts the farewell of the Boting Langi (heaven dwellers) and Lino (earth dwellers), with movements expressing the gentleness, loyalty, modesty and respect of Gowa women. Dancers wear the silk Baju Bodo and lipa' sa'be sarong, accompanied by seven male musicians playing the gandrang drum and puik-puik. A full performance can last nearly two hours.
kipas-pakarena.insight: Dancers are bound by strict rules - they may not open their eyes wide or raise their feet high - demanding great stamina to sustain the dance's restrained grace across its roughly two-hour, twelve-part structure (Indonesia-Tourism; Kompas).
kipas-pakarena.image_significance: Royal fan dance of the Gowa sultanate. A representative image shows gilded costume, angular hand poses and a temple or court setting — Gowa (Makassar), Indonesia.

cakalele.name: Cakalele
cakalele.era: Pre-colonial; tied to historic Moluccan warrior raids
cakalele.tagline: Moluccan war dance of dueling captains and shields
cakalele.profile: Cakalele (spelled tjakalele by the Dutch) is a war dance from the Maluku Islands of Indonesia (Wikipedia). It is performed by men, two of whom represent opposing captains while others are supporting warriors; after an opening ritual the captains engage in a mock duel with a spear (sanokat) and a long parang (lopu), while supporters carry a parang and a long shield (salawaku). Dancers wear full warrior costume and move to the rhythm of the tifa drum, gong and suling (fife). The dance originated as a way for warriors to celebrate after a successful raid and survives today as a welcoming and ceremonial dance honoring ancestors.
cakalele.insight: Hybrid versions of cakalele spread across eastern Indonesia, giving rise to related war dances such as the Minahasan Kabasaran of North Sulawesi (Wikipedia).
cakalele.image_significance: Maluku war dance with parang & shield. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — Maluku, Indonesia.

likok-pulo.name: Likok Pulo
likok-pulo.tagline: Acehnese seated island dance for Islamic preaching
likok-pulo.profile: Likok Pulo is a traditional Acehnese seated group dance from Pulo Aceh - specifically Pulo Nasi/Pulau Breuh (Beras Island) at the northern tip of Sumatra (Wikipedia; ISBI Aceh). 'Likok' means dance movement and 'Pulo' means island. It was created around 1849 by an Arab Muslim cleric (named in sources as Syech Ahmad Badroen/Badron) who was stranded on the island and used the dance for Islamic preaching (dakwah). Performed by men seated shoulder to shoulder in a line, with a leader (syekh/ceh) in the middle and two rapa'i drummers, it uses body percussion and the wooden 'boh likok' prop to keep tempo, accompanied by Acehnese verses praising God. Performances are often held at night after planting or harvest.
likok-pulo.insight: Like the related Saman, Likok Pulo replaces forbidden hand-clapping with body percussion and the boh likok pipe to align with Islamic propriety, and has shifted from a dakwah medium to an educational and tourism performance (Grokipedia; ISBI Aceh).
likok-pulo.image_significance: Seated Acehnese body-percussion dance. A representative image shows gilded costume, angular hand poses and a temple or court setting — Aceh, Indonesia.
